title: Integers as products of set differences
competition: South African Mathematics Olympiad — Senior Final
statement:
Let $A$ be a set of real numbers satisfying the following:
(a) $\sqrt{n^2+1} \in A$ for all positive integers $n$;
(b) if $x \in A$ and $y \in A$, then $x - y \in A$.
Prove that every integer can be written as a product of two different elements in $A$.
solution:
We first observe some natural consequences of property (b):
(i) $0 \in A$, since if $x \in A$ is arbitrary, then $0 = x - x \in A$.
(ii) If $x \in A$, then $-x = 0 - x \in A$.
(iii) If $x, y \in A$, then $x + y = x - (-y) \in A$.
(iv) If $x \in A$, then $kx \in A$ for any integer $k$. This follows easily by induction on $k$ (for positive $k$), using (iii). For negative $k$, apply (ii). For $k = 0$, use (i).

So now we know that $k\sqrt{m^2+1} + l\sqrt{n^2+1} \in A$ for all integers $k$ and $l$, and all positive integers $m$ and $n$.
Let us first try to write the integer 1 as a product of two different elements in $A$: We can find (by inspection) positive integers $k, l, m, n$ such that $1 = k^2(m^2+1) - l^2(n^2+1)$, for example, $k=3, m=1, l=1, n=4$. (There are many other possibilities as well.) Hence,
$$
\begin{aligned}
1 &= 3^2(1^2 + 1) - 1^2(4^2 + 1) \\
&= (3\sqrt{1^2 + 1} - 1\sqrt{4^2 + 1})(3\sqrt{1^2 + 1} + 1\sqrt{4^2 + 1}),
\end{aligned}
$$
a product of two different elements of $A$.
If $p$ is an arbitrary integer, then we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
p = p \cdot 1 &= p \cdot (3\sqrt{1^2+1} - 1\sqrt{4^2+1})(3\sqrt{1^2+1} + 1\sqrt{4^2+1}) \\
&= (3p\sqrt{1^2+1} - p\sqrt{4^2+1})(3\sqrt{1^2+1} + 1\sqrt{4^2+1}),
\end{aligned}
$$
again a product of two elements of $A$. These two elements of $A$ are indeed different, since if $3p\sqrt{1^2+1} - p\sqrt{4^2+1} = 3\sqrt{1^2+1} + 1\sqrt{4^2+1}$, then we would have $p = 35 + 6\sqrt{34}$, which is not an integer.
ratingReason: Closure under subtraction must be converted to integer linear combinations, then a deliberately chosen difference of squares produces 1.
notes: Difficulty is an editorial estimate based on this problem and its solution, not the question number. Source transcription: MathNet; original organiser credited in provenance. Original organiser: South African Mathematics Foundation.

title: Injectivity of multiplicative functional equation
competition: South African Mathematics Olympiad — Senior Final
statement:
Let $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}_0$ be a function that satisfies
$$
f(mn) = mf(n) + nf(m)
$$
for all positive integers $m, n$ and $f(2024) = 10120$.
Prove that there are two integers $m, n$ with $m \neq n$ such that $f(m) = f(n)$.
solution:
By setting $n = 1$, we obtain $mf(1) = 0$ for all $m$, so $f(1) = 0$. Next we notice that since every positive integer can be written as a product of prime numbers, the function $f$ is determined completely by its value on the primes. If there exists $m \ge 2$ such that $f(m) = 0$, then $f(m) = f(1)$ and we are done. Thus assume for all $m \ge 2$ that $f(m) \ge 1$.
Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}
f(2024) &= f(8 \cdot 11 \cdot 23) = 23f(8 \cdot 11) + 88f(23) = 23(11f(8) + 8f(11)) + 88f(23) \\
&= 253f(8) + 184f(11) + 88f(23).
\end{aligned}
$$
To study $f(8)$, we instead derive a general formula for perfect powers:
$$
f(a^2) = af(a) + af(a) = 2af(a),
$$
$$
f(a^3) = a^2f(a) + af(a^2) = 3a^2f(a).
$$
We assume as inductive hypothesis that
$$
f(a^n) = na^{n-1}f(a),
$$
and prove it for $n+1$ by
$$
f(a^{n+1}) = f(a^n \cdot a) = af(a^n) + a^n f(a) = a(na^{n-1})f(a) + a^n f(a) = (n+1)a^n f(a).
$$
Thus
$$
10120 = f(2024) = 253(3 \cdot 2^2)f(2) + 184f(11) + 88f(23) = 3036f(2) + 184f(11) + 88f(23). \quad (1)
$$
Considering this equation modulo 11, we conclude that $f(11)$ is divisible by 11, and by the assumption that $f(11) \ge 1$, we conclude that $f(11) \ge 11$. Similarly, working modulo 23 tells us that $f(23)$ is divisible by 23 and thus $f(23) \ge 23$. Finally, working modulo 8 tells us that $4f(2)$ is divisible by 8, so $f(2) \ge 2$. Thus the right hand-side of (1) is greater than or equal to
$$
3036 \cdot 2 + 184 \cdot 11 + 88 \cdot 23 = 10120.
$$
Since we have equality, we must conclude that
$$
f(2) = 2, \quad f(11) = 11 \quad \text{and} \quad f(23) = 23.
$$
Our only hope to find two integers $m$ and $n$ for which $f(m) = f(n)$ is to use the information just obtained. Thus, we set
$$
m = 2^a 11^b 23^c \quad n = 2^d 11^e 23^f.
$$
Intuitively we hope to find values of **d**, **e**, **f** that are close to **a**, **b**, **c** (e.g. differ by 1) and then solve for values **a**, **b**, **c** that happen to work. We notice that $2 \cdot 11 = 22$ is close to 23, so let us study
$$
\begin{align*} 
f(22^a 23^c) &= 23^c f(22^a) + 22^a f(23^c) \\ 
&= 23^c (a \cdot 22^{a-1} \cdot f(22)) + 22^a (c \cdot 23^{c-1} \cdot f(23)) \\ 
&= 23^c (a \cdot 22^{a-1} \cdot (2f(11) + 11f(2))) + 22^a (c \cdot 23^{c-1} \cdot 23) \\ 
&= 23^c (a \cdot 22^{a-1} \cdot 44) + 22^a (c \cdot 23^{c-1} \cdot 23) \\ 
&= (2a + c) 22^a 23^c 
\end{align*}
$$
Now we compare $f(22^a 23^{b+1})$ with $f(22^{a+1} 23^b)$ and hope to find values of **a**, **b** for which they are equal.
$$
\begin{aligned} 
f(22^a 23^{b+1}) &= (2a + b + 1) 22^a 23^{b+1}, \\ 
f(22^{a+1} 23^b) &= (2(a + 1) + b) 22^{a+1} 23^b. 
\end{aligned}
$$
Thus if we can find values of **a**, **b** such that
$$
2a + b + 1 = 22 \quad \text{and} \quad 2a + b + 2 = 23
$$
we would be done. Luckily there are many such pairs, for example
$(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}) \in \{(1, 19), (2, 17), (3, 15), (4, 13), (5, 11), (6, 9), (7, 7), (8, 5), (9, 3), (10, 1)\}$.
ratingReason: The product-rule functional equation first forces values at three primes by congruences, then needs an engineered equality between two multiplicative expressions.

title: Lattice coloring with L-shaped punch
competition: South African Mathematics Olympiad — Senior Final
statement: Each of the lattice points $(x, y)$ ($x$ and $y$ integers) in the plane can be coloured black or white. A single strike by an L-shaped punch changes the colour of the four lattice points $(a, b)$, $(a+1, b)$, $(a, b+1)$ and $(a, b+2)$. All lattice points are initially coloured white. Prove that after any number of strikes, the number of black lattice points will be either zero or greater than or equal to four.
solution:
When the lattice points $(a, b)$, $(a+1, b)$, $(a, b+1)$ and $(a, b+2)$ change colour after a single strike by the punch, let us call the point $(a, b)$ the corner point of the strike.

We first show (by induction on the number of strikes) that, after any finite number of strikes, there will always be an even number of black lattice points. After the first strike, four points (an even number) will be black. Suppose that after $n$ strikes, for some $n \ge 1$, an even number, say $2m$, of black lattice points $X = \{(x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2), \dots, (x_{2m}, y_{2m})\}$ remain. For the $(n+1)$-th strike, with corner point $(a, b)$, put $Y = \{(a, b), (a+1, b), (a, b+1), (a, b+2)\}$. Let $|X \cap Y| = k \in \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}$, where $|S|$ denotes the size of a set $S$. Then, after strike number $n+1$, the number of black points will be $|(X \cup Y) \setminus (X \cap Y)|$, which is $|X| + |Y| - 2k = 2m + 4 - 2k$, an even number. This completes the induction.

We now show that it never happens that exactly two black points remain after any finite number of strikes, which will solve the problem.

First, we observe that the moment the same corner point $(a, b)$ appears twice in a series of strikes, we can just as well ignore these two strikes, since the colours of the points in the set $\{(a, b), (a+1, b), (a, b+1), (a, b+2)\}$ will remain the same after two strikes with corner point $(a, b)$, irrespective of where they appear in the series of strikes. Hence, we may assume that all the corner points in the finite series of strikes are different (each appearing exactly once).

Let $X = \{(x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2), \dots, (x_{2m}, y_{2m})\}$ be the total number of black lattice points that remain after these strikes.

Amongst the $y$-coordinates $y_1, y_2, \dots, y_{2m}$, let $y'$ be the smallest. Say $y_{i_1}, y_{i_2}, \dots, y_{i_k}$ are all the $y$-coordinates equal to $y'$. We assume them to be ordered such that $x_{i_1} < x_{i_2} < \dots < x_{i_k}$. It follows that, amongst these points, the point $(x_{i_1}, y')$ is the corner point of a strike, while $(x_{i_k}, y')$ is not (with $(x_{i_k} - 1, y')$ the corner point of the strike producing $(x_{i_k}, y')$). So the two points $(x_{i_1}, y')$ and $(x_{i_k}, y')$ cannot be the same, since $(x_{i_1}, y')$ is a corner point of a strike, while $(x_{i_k}, y')$ is not. Hence, there are at least two black points with $y$-coordinates equal to $y'$.

Analogously, amongst the $x$-coordinates $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2m}$, let $x'$ be the smallest. Say $x_{j_1}, x_{j_2}, \dots, x_{j_m}$ are all the $x$-coordinates equal to $x'$. We assume them to be ordered such that

$y_{j_1} < y_{j_2} < \cdots < y_{j_m}$.

It follows that, amongst these points, the point $(x', y_{j_1})$ is the corner point of a strike, while $(x', y_{j_m})$ is not (with $(x', y_{j_m} - 2)$ the corner point of the strike producing $(x', y_{j_m})$). So the two points $(x', y_{j_1})$ and $(x', y_{j_m})$ cannot be the same, since $(x', y_{j_1})$ is a corner point of a strike, while $(x', y_{j_m})$ is not. Hence, there are at least two black points with $x$-coordinates equal to $x'$.

We see that there are at least three black points in the subset $\{(x_{i_1}, y'), (x_{i_k}, y'), (x', y_{j_1}), (x', y_{j_m})\}$ of $X$. (There is a possibility that $(x_{i_1}, y') = (x', y_{j_1})$.) Therefore, since $X$ contains an even number of points, we conclude that $|X| \ge 4$.

Recall that we can strike the punch twice at corner point $(0,0)$, say, to obtain a scenario where there are no black points after a series of strikes.

Our conclusion is that the number of black lattice points after a finite number of strikes is an even number that is either $0$, or greater than or equal to $4$.
ratingReason: Parity alone is insufficient: cancelling repeated punches and examining extremal rows and columns forces at least three surviving cells.

title: Centers of Tangent Circles Configuration
competition: South African Mathematics Olympiad — Senior Final
statement:
Consider three circles $\Gamma_1, \Gamma_2$ and $\Gamma_3$, with centres $O_1, O_2$ and $O_3$, respectively, such that each pair of circles is externally tangent. Suppose we have another circle $\Gamma$ with centre $O$ on the line segment $O_1O_3$ such that $\Gamma_1, \Gamma_2$ and $\Gamma_3$ are each internally tangent to $\Gamma$.
Show that $\angle O_1O_2O_3$ measures less than $90^\circ$.
solution:
Write the radii of $\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2,\Gamma_3$ as $a,b,c$, and put $s=a+c$. As the large-circle centre is on $O_1O_3$, the two endpoint circles occupy a diameter: its radius is $s$, with $OO_1=c$ and $OO_3=a$.

Take $O_1=(0,0)$, $O_3=(s,0)$ and $O=(c,0)$, and write $O_2=(u,v)$. External and internal tangency give
$$u^2+v^2=(a+b)^2,\quad (u-s)^2+v^2=(b+c)^2,\quad (u-c)^2+v^2=(s-b)^2.$$
Subtracting the first two gives $u=a+b(a-c)/s$. Substitution into the third then yields
$$b=\frac{acs}{a^2+ac+c^2}.$$
In particular $bs>ac$. Therefore
$$(a+b)^2+(b+c)^2-(a+c)^2=2(b^2+bs-ac)>0.$$
By the cosine rule in $O_1O_2O_3$, the angle at $O_2$ is strictly less than $90^\circ$.
ratingReason: The tangency constraints impose a non-obvious relation between the three radii; combining it with the cosine rule proves strict acuteness.

title: Integer functional equation with quadratic RHS
competition: South African Mathematics Olympiad — Senior Final
statement:
Find all functions $f$ from integers to integers such that
$$
f(m+n) + f(m-n) - 2f(m) = 6mn^2
$$
for all integers $m$ and $n$.
solution:
First note that if we replace $f(x)$ by $f(x) + ax + c$ for some constants $a$ and $c$, then we get another solution. Thus we may assume for now that $f(0) = 0$ and $f(1) = 1$.
Let $P(m, n)$ be the statement that was given. Then $P(0, n)$ gives
$$
f(n) + f(-n) - 2f(0) = 0
$$
and since $f(0) = 0$, we get $f(-n) = -f(n)$. Then taking $P(n, m)$,
$$
f(m+n) + f(n-m) - 2f(n) = 6m^2n
$$
and subtracting this from $P(m, n)$ gives
$$
2f(m-n) + 2f(n) - 2f(m) = 6mn(n-m).
$$
Setting $n = -1$, dividing by 2 and rearranging gives
$$
f(m+1) = f(m) + f(1) + 3m(m+1).
$$
The first few values of $m$ tell us:
$$
f(2) = 8, \quad f(3) = 27, \quad f(4) = 64.
$$
We hypothesise for an inductive argument that $f(n) = n^3$ and show that
$$
f(n+1) = f(1) + f(n) + 3n(n+1) = n^3 + 3n^2 + 3n + 1 = (n+1)^3.
$$
Thus $f(n) = n^3$ for all positive integers, and hence by $f(-n) = -f(n)$ also for all negative integers.
Now incorporating our initial remark, we find that all solutions are of the form $f(n) = n^3 + an + c$ for some integer constants $a$ and $c$.
ratingReason: Subtracting the expected cubic reduces the problem to a discrete affine equation; the integer-domain recurrence must be proved in both directions.
notes: Difficulty is an editorial estimate based on this problem and its solution, not the question number. Source transcription: MathNet; original organiser credited in provenance. Original organiser: South African Mathematics Foundation.

statement: For which integers $n>2$ can the edges of an $n$-gon be labelled $1,\ldots,n$, each once, so that the sums of the two labels meeting at each vertex form an arithmetic progression after rearrangement?
solution:
Exactly the odd integers work. The sum of the vertex sums is $n(n+1)$. If the progression begins at $a$ and has difference $d\ge0$, then $2a+(n-1)d=2n+2$. Since $a\ge3$, a positive difference must be $d=1$. Difference zero is impossible: equal adjacent sums would force the edge labels to repeat every two edges. Thus $a=(n+3)/2$, so $n$ is odd.

For $n=2k-1$, place the edge labels cyclically in the order
$$k,\ 2k-1,\ k-1,\ 2k-2,\ k-2,\ldots,\ k+1,\ 1.$$
Their neighbouring sums are precisely $k+1,k+2,\ldots,3k-1$.
ratingReason: The sum constraint gives necessity, but an explicit cyclic construction is also needed.
notes: Australian Mathematics Trust problem. Mathematical statement paraphrased; displayed exposition independently written. Difficulty assessed from this problem and its solution.

statement: Given any nonzero real polynomial $f$, prove that some real polynomial $g$ makes $fg$ have exactly $2023$ more positive coefficients than negative coefficients. Zero coefficients do not count.
solution:
Write the lowest and highest nonzero terms of $f$ as $c_a x^a,c_bx^b$. If $a=b$, the claim follows immediately by multiplying by a suitably signed sum of $2023$ monomials. Otherwise choose $\lambda>0$ with $c_a-\lambda c_b\ne0$, and put $h=x^{b-a}-\lambda$.

In $hf$, the low copy of the coefficients of $f$ has its signs reversed, while the high copy retains them. Apart from their shared endpoint, these sign counts cancel. Consequently, the number of positive coefficients minus negative coefficients in $hf$ is
$$\operatorname{sgn}(c_a-\lambda c_b)-\operatorname{sgn}(c_a)+\operatorname{sgn}(c_b),$$
which is either $1$ or $-1$. Choose a sign $\varepsilon$ making it $1$. If $D>\deg(hf)$, then
$$g=\varepsilon h(1+x^D+x^{2D}+\cdots+x^{2022D})$$
creates $2023$ disjoint copies of the coefficient list, giving the result.
ratingReason: A carefully shifted difference cancels almost every coefficient sign; separated copies then amplify the imbalance.
notes: Australian Mathematics Trust problem. Mathematical statement paraphrased; displayed exposition independently written. Difficulty assessed from this problem and its solution.

statement: In acute triangle $ABC$, let $D$ be the foot of the altitude from $A$. Choose $P\in AB$ and $Q\in AC$ with $PQ\parallel BC$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $PQ$. Let $X$ be the intersection of segment $DM$ with circle $APQ$ lying inside $ABC$. Prove $\angle AXB=\angle AXC$.
solution: The linked paper contains the official worked solution. Open “Source solution” below to read it.

statement: A finite interval of positive integers has this property: whenever two subsets $C,U$ satisfy $|C|=|U|+1$, their sums satisfy $\sum C>\sum U$. The subsets may overlap. Prove that the interval contains at most one perfect square.
solution:
If it contained two squares, it would contain $x^2$ and $(x+1)^2$ for some positive integer $x$, together with all intervening integers. Take
$$C=\{x^2,x^2+1,\ldots,x^2+x\},\qquad U=\{x^2+x+1,\ldots,x^2+2x\}.$$
Their sizes differ by one, but
$$\sum C=(x+1)x^2+\frac{x(x+1)}2
= x(x^2+x)+\frac{x(x+1)}2=\sum U,$$
a contradiction.
ratingReason: The central insight is to build two equal-sum blocks between consecutive squares with sizes differing by one.

statement: Fix a parallelogram $ABCD$. A point $E$ moves along the interior of $AB$. If $K,L$ are the circumcentres of $ADE,BCE$, respectively, prove that the length $KL$ is constant.
solution:
Choose $A=(0,0),B=(s,0),D=(u,v),C=(s+u,v)$, with $v\ne0$, and put $E=(t,0)$. The perpendicular bisectors of $AE$ and $BE$ give the horizontal coordinates of the two centres. Equating their squared distances from the other vertices gives
$$K=\left(\frac t2,\frac{u^2+v^2-ut}{2v}\right),\quad L=\left(\frac{s+t}2,\frac{u^2+v^2+us-ut}{2v}\right).$$
Therefore $L-K=(s/2,us/(2v))$, independent of $t$.

statement: For every positive integer $n$, prove that at least $2023$ positive integers $k$ have their divisors partitionable into two sets $A,B$ with $\sum_{d\in A}d-\sum_{d\in B}d=n$.
solution:
In fact there are infinitely many such $k$. Signed sums of $1,2,\ldots,2^r$ attain every odd integer between $-(2^{r+1}-1)$ and $2^{r+1}-1$: choose the positive terms to have binary subset sum $(n+2^{r+1}-1)/2$. Thus odd $n$ works with every sufficiently large $k=2^r$.

For even $n$, use $k=3\cdot2^r$. Its divisors form two disjoint lists, $2^i$ and $3\cdot2^i$ for $0\le i\le r$. Give the first list signs summing to the odd number $n-3$, possible for all sufficiently large $r$. On the second list use the signs
$$3\cdot2^r-3(1+2+\cdots+2^{r-1})=3.$$
Together the signed divisor sum is $n$.
ratingReason: Two different divisor constructions are needed for odd and even targets; binary signed sums provide the common mechanism.

statement: The cards $1,2,\ldots,2023$ are hidden in an unknown order. Before each card is revealed, choose a positive integer $t$. Score $t$ if that card is at least $t$, and zero otherwise. What is the largest total score that can be guaranteed, allowing choices to depend on previous cards?
solution:
The answer is $1012^2$. Always choosing $1012$ earns this amount, since exactly $1012$ cards meet the threshold.

For the upper bound, an adversary reveals the smallest remaining card whenever it is below the chosen threshold. Otherwise it reveals the largest remaining card, and the turn scores at most the smallest remaining value. The cards revealed on successful turns therefore form a descending list $2023,2022,\ldots,b$ for some $b$. On every such turn the score is at most $b$, which has not yet been removed. Hence the total is at most
$$b(2024-b)\le1012^2.$$
For any fixed adaptive strategy these choices produce one valid ordering of the deck, so the bound applies to every strategy.

statement: Let $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ be positive real numbers. The score of a permutation $b_1,\ldots,b_n$ is $\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}b_i^2/b_{i+1}$. Prove that two permutations have scores differing by at least $3|a_1-a_n|$.
solution:
Sort the numbers as $x_1\ge\cdots\ge x_n$, and compare this order with its reverse. Their score difference is
$$\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\left(\frac{x_i^2}{x_{i+1}}-\frac{x_{i+1}^2}{x_i}\right)
=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}(x_i-x_{i+1})\frac{x_i^2+x_ix_{i+1}+x_{i+1}^2}{x_ix_{i+1}}.$$
Since the last fraction is at least $3$, this is at least $3(x_1-x_n)\ge3|a_1-a_n|$.

statement: How many black-and-white colourings of a $2024\times2024$ grid have an even number of black side-neighbours at every cell? Only cells inside the grid are counted as neighbours.
solution:
More generally an $n\times n$ grid has $2^n$ such colourings. Work over $\mathbf F_2$, encode a black cell by $1$, and write row $i$ as a column vector $r_i$. Let $A$ be the adjacency matrix of the path with $n$ vertices, and set the outside rows $r_0=r_{n+1}=0$. The condition is
$$r_{i+1}=Ar_i+r_{i-1}.$$
Thus the first row determines every other row. It remains to check that every first row produces the required final zero row.

Let $D_j(x)$ be the characteristic polynomial of the path adjacency matrix of size $j$. Expansion of the tridiagonal determinant gives $D_0=1,D_1=x,D_j=xD_{j-1}+D_{j-2}$ over $\mathbf F_2$. The row recurrence gives $r_{n+1}=D_n(A)r_1=0$ by the Cayley–Hamilton theorem. All $2^n$ first rows therefore work; the answer is $2^{2024}$.

statement: Find all real polynomials $P$ positive on the positive real numbers such that $1/P(x)+1/P(y)+1/P(z)=1$ whenever $x,y,z>0$ and $xyz=1$.

An acyclic tournament therefore orders all vertices uniquely, with every edge directed forward. Conversely every ordering gives such a tournament. statement: Sixty pupils each name three different other pupils as friends. Must it be possible to split them into three classes of twenty so that every pupil shares a class with at least one of their named friends?

Their midpoint is $M=(1/u,0)$. Hence

Thus $MP$ is perpendicular to the radius through $P$, as required.

Put $d_i=a_{i+1}-a_i$. These are strictly decreasing integers with sum zero. Set $e_i=d_i-(50-i)$ for $1\le i\le99$. Since $d_i-d_{i+1}\ge1$, the sequence $e_i$ is nonincreasing; its sum is zero because $49+48+\cdots-49=0$.

statement: Let $B_n$ count binary strings of length $n$ in which every position has a neighbouring position equal to $1$. Find the smallest $n\ge2$ for which $20\mid B_n$.
solution:
The answer is $25$. The endpoint condition forces the second and penultimate entries to be $1$; internally, two entries at distance two cannot both be zero. Splitting into odd and even positions therefore separates the restrictions.

Let $F_0=0,F_1=1,F_{j+2}=F_{j+1}+F_j$. Binary strings of length $r$ with no consecutive zeros are counted by $F_{r+2}$, by separating strings ending in $1$ and in $10$. Hence
$$B_{2m}=F_{m+1}^2,\qquad B_{2m+1}=F_mF_{m+3}.$$
(The odd formula for $m=1$ follows directly.) The Fibonacci residues give $2\mid F_j$ exactly when $3\mid j$, and $5\mid F_j$ exactly when $5\mid j$; these follow by checking the repeating pairs modulo $2$ and $5$.

For even lengths, divisibility by $20$ first occurs at $m+1=15$, giving $28$. For odd lengths, the two Fibonacci factors have the same parity, so divisibility by $4$ occurs exactly when $3\mid m$. Divisibility by $5$ also requires $5\mid m$ or $5\mid m+3$. The smallest positive $m$ meeting both requirements is $12$, giving $n=25$.

statement: Put $f(x)=x^2-45x+2$. Find all integers $n\ge2$ for which precisely one of $f(1),\ldots,f(n)$ is divisible by $n$.
solution:
If $a$ is the unique root modulo $n$, then $45-a$ is another root, since $f(45-a)=f(a)$. Uniqueness gives $2a\equiv45\pmod n$. But
$$4f(a)=(2a-45)^2-2017,$$
so $n\mid2017$. The number $2017$ is prime (trial division by the primes at most $43$ suffices), and therefore $n=2017$.

Conversely modulo $2017$, the equation is $(2a-45)^2\equiv0$, which has exactly the one solution $a\equiv1031$. Thus $n=2017$ works.

statement: Find all functions $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ satisfying $f(xy+f(y))=y f(x)$ for every real $x,y$.
solution:
The solutions are $f\equiv0$ and $f(x)=1-x$. Both satisfy the equation directly.

For any other possibility, choose $a$ with $f(a)\ne0$. Keeping $x=a$ and varying $y$ shows that $f$ is surjective. Setting $x=0$ gives $f(f(y))=y f(0)$. Surjectivity of the left side forces $f(0)\ne0$, so this identity also implies that $f$ is injective.

At $y=1$ the identity gives $f(f(1))=f(0)$, hence $f(1)=0$. Finally the original equation with $x=1$ gives $f(y+f(y))=0=f(1)$. Injectivity yields $y+f(y)=1$, as claimed.

statement: Let $b_1>1$ be an integer and define $b_{n+1}=d(b_n)^2$, where $d(m)$ is the number of positive divisors of $m$. Prove that some term equals $9$.
solution:
Every term from $b_2$ onward is a square; a square has an odd number of divisors, so every term from $b_3$ onward is an odd square greater than one.

For an odd square $m=\prod p_i^{2e_i}$, its next term is $\prod(2e_i+1)^2$. For every odd prime $p$ and positive integer $e$, the elementary induction $p^e\ge3^e\ge2e+1$ holds, with equality only for $p=3,e=1$. Therefore $d(m)^2\le m$, with equality only when $m=9$. (Equality cannot involve two different primes, both equal to $3$.)

The positive terms thus strictly decrease from index three until reaching $9$, where they remain. Infinite strict descent is impossible.

statement: Rocks have positive integer masses totalling $2018$ kilograms, and cannot be split into two piles of $1009$ kilograms. What is the largest possible number of rocks?
solution:
The answer is $1009$, attained by $1009$ rocks of mass $2$, since no subset then has odd total mass.

Suppose there were $m>1009$ rocks. List them in any order and take the $m$ partial sums before each rock, starting with $0$, regarded modulo $2018$. They are distinct because the masses are positive and their total is $2018$. This set $S$ and its translate $S+1009$ have total size greater than $2018$, so they intersect. Two partial sums therefore differ by $1009$ modulo $2018$, and, lying between $0$ and $2017$, differ in absolute value by exactly $1009$. The intervening block of rocks is the forbidden half-mass pile.

statement: Three piles initially contain $2020$ stones each. A move chooses one pile, discards all others, and splits the chosen pile into two or three nonempty piles. Players alternate, and the player unable to move loses. Prove that the second player can force a win.
solution:
The second player always leaves every pile with size congruent to $1$ modulo $3$. This holds initially. Splitting such a pile into two or three parts cannot leave every part congruent to $1$, since their sum would then be $2$ or $0$ modulo $3$.

The second player chooses a part of size $s\not\equiv1\pmod3$. If $s\equiv2$, split it into $1,s-1$; if $s\equiv0$, split it into $1,1,s-2$. Each new pile is positive and congruent to $1$. Each second-player reply is legal. Since the total number of stones decreases whenever piles are discarded and no infinite sequence of proper splittings is possible, play ends with the first player unable to move.

The point $G=(u,uv/(u-1))$ lies on $BE$, as its parameter along $B+t(E-B)$ is $t=2u/(u-1)$. Moreover
$$C\cdot(G-A)=u(u+1)+\frac{uv^2}{u-1}=0,$$
using $v^2=1-u^2$. Therefore $AG$ is parallel to the tangent $CD$, so $G=F$. Since $F$ and $C$ have the same first coordinate, $CF$ is perpendicular to $AB$.

statement: Inside square $ABCD$, choose $P$. Two perpendicular lines through $P$ meet opposite sides $AB,CD$ at $W,Y$ and $BC,DA$ at $X,Z$, respectively. Determine the points $P$ for which $WXYZ$ is cyclic for every such pair of lines.

Exactly the points on either diagonal work. Take the unit square with $P=(x,y)$. For a unit direction vector $(s,t)$ along $WY$, the perpendicular direction along $XZ$ is $(-t,s)$. Intersections with the horizontal sides give

while intersections with the vertical sides give
$$PX\cdot PZ=\frac{x(1-x)}{t^2}.$$
The four points are cyclic precisely when these products agree. Thus the condition is independent of the choice of valid directions and equivalent to
$$y(1-y)=x(1-x),\qquad (x-y)(1-x-y)=0.$$
These are exactly the two diagonals. Axis-parallel lines are valid for every interior $P$, so necessity is also established.

statement: For a positive integer $r$, set $n=16^{3^r}-4^{3^r}+1$. Prove that $n$ divides $2^{n-1}-1$.

Put $y=4^{3^r}$, so $n=y^2-y+1$. The factorization
$$(y+1)n=y^3+1=2^{2\cdot3^{r+1}}+1$$
gives $2^{4\cdot3^{r+1}}\equiv1\pmod n$.

It remains to show that this exponent divides $n-1=y(y-1)$. Certainly $4\mid y$. Repeated difference-of-cubes factorization gives
$$4^{3^r}-1=(4-1)\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}\left(16^{3^i}+4^{3^i}+1\right).$$
Every factor displayed is divisible by $3$, so $3^{r+1}\mid y-1$. Hence $4\cdot3^{r+1}\mid n-1$. Raising the earlier congruence to the resulting integer power proves the claim.

statement: For a positive integer $n$, let $f(n)$ be its distance from the nearest power of $2$, and let $S(n)$ be the number of iterations of $f$ first needed to reach $0$. Find (a) the smallest $n$ with $S(n)=2022$; (b) the largest possible number of consecutive positive integers having the same stopping time.
solution:
For (a), the answer is $(2^{4043}+1)/3$. Let $m_k$ be the smallest number of stopping time $k$. We have $m_1=1$. For a positive distance $d$, let $P$ be the smallest power of two at least $2d$. The smallest positive integer whose distance from its nearest power of two is $d$ is $P+d$: in every smaller interval between consecutive powers, the maximum distance is less than $d$, and within the next interval $P+d$ is the first point attaining it. Thus this smallest preimage is an increasing function of $d$.

It follows inductively that
$$m_k=\frac{2^{2k-1}+1}{3}.$$
Indeed, for $d=m_{k-1}$ the power $P$ above is $2^{2k-3}$, so $m_k=P+m_{k-1}$. No smaller preimage can have stopping time $k$, because its image would be at least $m_{k-1}$ and the smallest-preimage function is increasing.

For (b), the answer is three, attained by $5,6,7$, whose images are $1,2,1$. Suppose four consecutive integers of equal stopping time exist, and choose such a block with smallest first term. Its stopping time cannot be one, and the block cannot contain a power of two. It therefore lies strictly between consecutive powers $2^a,2^{a+1}$.

The function $f$ increases by one up to the midpoint $M=3\cdot2^{a-1}$ and decreases by one afterwards. If the block does not straddle this midpoint, its four images are four consecutive smaller positive integers of equal stopping time, contradicting minimality. If it straddles the midpoint, it contains $M$ and a neighbour. For $a\ge3$, their images are $2^{a-1}$ and $2^{a-1}-1$, of stopping times one and two respectively, again impossible. For $a\le2$, the open interval between the two powers contains at most three integers. This exhausts the cases.
ratingReason: The exact minimum needs a monotone inverse-distance argument; the consecutive-run bound needs a second descent argument with careful treatment of midpoint folds.

statement: Let $ABC$ be an acute scalene triangle with orthocentre $H$. The altitudes from $B,C$ meet the internal bisector of $\angle BAC$ at $D,E$, respectively. The tangents at $D,E$ to circle $DEH$ meet at $X$. Prove $BX=CX$.

Put $A=(0,0)$ and use the angle bisector as the horizontal axis. Write
$$B=(uc,us),\quad C=(vc,-vs),\quad c^2+s^2=1,$$
where $u,v>0$, $c,s>0$, and $t=c^2-s^2>0$ because angle $A$ is acute. The stated nondegenerate configuration requires $u\ne v$. The altitude equations are $cx-sy=ut$ and $cx+sy=vt$, giving
$$D=(ut/c,0),\ E=(vt/c,0),\ H=(h,q),$$
where $h=(u+v)t/(2c)$ and $q=(v-u)t/(2s)$.

The centre of circle $DEH$ has form $(h,k)$. Put $d=(v-u)t/(2c)$, the signed half-length of $DE$. Equality of the squared radii to $D$ and $H$ gives
$$d^2+k^2=(q-k)^2,\qquad k=\frac{(v-u)t^2}{4sc^2}.$$
The tangents at the two horizontally symmetric points $D,E$ meet on $x=h$. The tangent equation at $D$ then gives $-k(X_y-k)=d^2+k^2$, so
$$X=(h,-d^2/k)=\left(\frac{(u+v)t}{2c},(u-v)s\right).$$
Finally,
$$2X\cdot(B-C)=(u^2-v^2)(t+2s^2)=u^2-v^2=|B|^2-|C|^2.$$
Expanding $|X-B|^2-|X-C|^2$ now gives zero, proving $BX=CX$.

statement: In acute triangle $ABC$, let $H$ be the orthocentre and $D,E,F$ the altitude feet on $BC,CA,AB$. Set $G=EF\cap AD$. If $I$ is the antipode of $A$ on the circumcircle and $J=AI\cap BC$, prove $HI\parallel GJ$.

Choose $A=(0,0),B=(u,v),C=(w,v)$, where $v>0$ and $u<0<w$. Put $q=v^2-uw>0$. The altitude through $B$ gives
$$H=(0,(v^2+uw)/v),$$
and the circumcircle centre gives $I=(u+w,q/v)$. Therefore
$$J=(v^2(u+w)/q,v).$$
Both $E,F$ lie on the circles with diameters $AH$ and $BC$. Subtracting their circle equations gives their common chord line
$$(u+w)x+(q/v)y=v^2+uw.$$
Consequently $G=(0,v(v^2+uw)/q)$, and
$$J-G=\frac{v^2}{q}\left(u+w,-\frac{2uw}{v}\right)=\frac{v^2}{q}(I-H).$$
The asserted parallelism follows.

statement: Classify prime powers $a$ and integers $n\ge2$ for which $a^n(a-1)+1$ is a square.
solution:
The solutions are $(a,n)=(2,3)$ and $(4,2)$, giving squares $9$ and $49$.

Write $m^2-1=a^n(a-1)$ with $m>1$. If $a=p^r$ for an odd prime $p$, then all of $p^{rn}$ divides one of $m-1,m+1$, since their gcd divides $2$. Thus $m\ge a^n-1$. Squaring and comparing gives $a^n\le a+1$, impossible for $a\ge3,n\ge2$.

If $a$ is a power of two, then $m$ is odd. Exactly one of $m-1,m+1$ has 2-adic valuation one, so the other is divisible by $a^n/2$. Hence $m\ge a^n/2-1$. Comparing squares now yields
$$a^{2n}/4-a^n\le a^n(a-1),\qquad a^{n-1}\le4.$$
Only $(2,2),(2,3),(4,2)$ remain, and direct substitution excludes $(2,2)$.

statement: A move on a binary string of length $n$ replaces two equal neighbouring bits by their complements. What is the largest family of strings in which no two can be transformed into one another by such moves?
solution:
The answer is $n+1$. Complement every other position in every string. Under this bijection, a legal move becomes an adjacent swap $01\leftrightarrow10$: originally equal neighbours become unequal because exactly one position was complemented.

Adjacent swaps preserve the number of ones, and any two binary strings with the same number of ones can be connected by adjacent swaps, by moving all ones to the left. Thus the original move system has exactly one equivalence class for each transformed number of ones $0,1,\ldots,n$. Taking one representative from each class attains $n+1$, and no larger family is possible.

If they are parallel, the midpoints of both pairs of projected points lie on the same perpendicular diameter of the original circle. statement: Find all six-digit positive integers $N$ for which every positive power of $N$ ends in the same six digits as $N$.

statement: Find all $f:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z$ with $f(1)=1$ and $f(x+y)+f(x-y)=\max\{f(2x),2f(y)\}$ for all integers $x,y$.
solution:
The solutions are $f(n)=1$ and $f(n)=|n|$. Write $c=f(0)$. The case $y=0$ gives $2f(x)=\max(f(2x),2c)$, so $f(x)\ge c$. Taking $x=y=0$ gives $c\ge0$; taking $x=1,y=0$ gives $c\le1$ and $f(2)\le2$. Hence $c=0$ or $1$.

With $x=0$, the equation yields $f(-y)=f(y)$, since $f(y)\ge c\ge0$. With $x=y=1$ it gives $f(2)=2-c$. Finally $x=1$ gives
$$f(y+1)+f(y-1)=\max(2-c,2f(y)).$$
Starting from $f(0)=c,f(1)=1$, this recurrence forces $f(n)=n$ for $n\ge0$ when $c=0$, and $f(n)=1$ when $c=1$. Evenness determines negative indices. The constant solution is immediate; for absolute values use $|x+y|+|x-y|=2\max(|x|,|y|)$.

statement: Intervals have endpoints in $\{1,\ldots,2024\}$, distinct positive lengths, and none contains another. What is the maximum possible number of intervals?
solution:
The answer is $1012$. For $m$ intervals, order their left endpoints $l_1<\cdots<l_m$. Their right endpoints must also increase strictly, since otherwise one interval would contain another. Thus $l_i\ge i$ and $r_i\le2024-m+i$, giving
$$1\le r_i-l_i\le2024-m.$$
There are $m$ distinct lengths in this range, so $m\le2024-m$, or $m\le1012$.

The intervals $[i,2i]$ for $1\le i\le1012$ achieve equality: both endpoints increase, and the lengths are the distinct integers $1,\ldots,1012$.

statement: Find all functions $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ satisfying $f(x^2)-yf(y)=f(x+y)(f(x)-y)$ for all real $x,y$.
solution:
The solutions are $f\equiv0$, $f\equiv1$, and $f(x)=x$. Setting $x=0$ gives $f(0)=f(0)f(y)$, so if $f(0)\ne0$ then $f\equiv1$.

Now suppose $f(0)=0$. Taking $y=0$ gives $f(x^2)=f(x)^2$, and taking $y=-x$ gives $f(x)^2=-xf(-x)$. Applying the latter to $-x$ as well shows that, for each nonzero $x$, either $f(x)=0$ or $f(x)=x$: if both values are nonzero, substitution yields $f(x)^3=x^3$.

statement: Find all $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ satisfying $f(x)f(y)+f(x+y)=xy$ for all real $x,y$.
solution:
The solutions are $f(x)=x-1$ and $f(x)=-x-1$. Taking $y=0$ gives $f(x)(f(0)+1)=0$. The zero function fails the original equation, so $f(0)=-1$.

Evaluate $f(x+y+z)$ first by grouping $x+y$ and $z$, then by grouping $x$ and $y+z$. Substituting the original identity and cancelling gives
$$xy(1+f(z))=yz(1+f(x)).$$
Set $y=z=1$. Then $f(x)+1=x(f(1)+1)$, so $f(x)=cx-1$ for some real $c$. Substitution into the original equation forces $c^2=1$. Both resulting functions satisfy it.

statement: For positive integers $n$, let $P(n)=n\prod_{j=1}^{16}(jn+1)$. Find $\gcd(P(1),P(2),\ldots,P(2016))$.

No larger prime can divide the gcd, since $P(1)=17!$. For each listed prime $p$, take $n=p$, which is among the permitted inputs. All factors $jp+1$ are coprime to $p$, so $P(p)$ contains only one factor of $p$. Hence the gcd is exactly the stated squarefree product.

statement: For positive integer $n$, count positive integer pairs $(x,y)$ with $x^2-y^2=100\cdot30^{2n}$, and prove that this count is never a square.

The integers $x,y$ have the same parity, so write $x-y=2u,x+y=2v$ with positive $u<v$. Then
$$uv=25\cdot30^{2n}=2^{2n}3^{2n}5^{2n+2}.$$
This is a square and has $(2n+1)^2(2n+3)$ divisors. Its unequal factor pairs number
$$\frac{(2n+1)^2(2n+3)-1}{2}=(n+1)(4n^2+6n+1).$$
The two factors on the right are coprime, since the second is congruent to $-1$ modulo $n+1$. If the count were square, each factor would be square. But
$$(2n+1)^2<4n^2+6n+1<(2n+2)^2$$
for $n>0$, a contradiction.

statement: A round-robin chess tournament has twice as many girls as boys, with no draws. Girls win $7/9$ as many games as boys. How many players are there?

Among $1\le b\le11$, the only possibility is $b=11$: for odd $b$, one needs $3b\equiv1\pmod{32}$, giving $b\equiv11$; for even $b$, the odd factor $3b-1$ requires $32\mid b$, impossible in this range. Thus there are $33$ players. This is achievable by letting every boy beat every girl: the girls' $231$ internal wins and the boys' $55+242=297$ wins have ratio $7:9$.

statement: A collection of primes, with repetition allowed, has product equal to ten times its sum. Determine the collection.

The product is divisible by ten, so remove one $2$ and one $5$. If the remaining primes are $q_1,\ldots,q_r$, their product must satisfy

statement: Find all integer pairs $(m,n)$ for which both $\displaystyle\frac{m^2+n}{n^2-m}$ and $\displaystyle\frac{n^2+m}{m^2-n}$ are defined and integers.
solution:
The solutions are $(t,-t)$ for every integer $|t|\ge2$, together with
$$(-1,-1),\ (\pm1,0),\ (0,\pm1),\ (1,2),\ (2,1),\ (2,2),\ (2,3),\ (3,2),\ (3,3).$$
The condition is symmetric in $m,n$. First suppose both absolute values are at least two. If $|m|\ge|n|+2$, then
$$|n^2+m|\le n^2+|m|<m^2-|n|\le m^2-n.$$
The second fraction therefore lies strictly between $-1$ and $1$, and must be zero. This gives $m=-n^2$. The first fraction then equals $(n^3+1)/(2n)$, whose integrality forces $n\mid1$, a contradiction. By symmetry the two absolute values differ by at most one.

If $|m|=|n|=t\ge2$, write $m=\varepsilon t,n=\delta t$ with signs $\varepsilon,\delta$. The fractions become $(t+\delta)/(t-\varepsilon)$ and $(t+\varepsilon)/(t-\delta)$. Opposite signs always work; two negative signs never do; two positive signs work only for $t=2,3$.

For absolute values differing by one, symmetry lets us write $m=\varepsilon(t+1),n=\delta t$, $t\ge2$. The second fraction is
$$\frac{t^2+\varepsilon(t+1)}{(t+1)^2-\delta t}.$$
Unless both signs are positive, this is strictly between zero and one. With both positive it is one, and the first fraction is $1+(4t+2)/(t^2-t-1)$. Checking $t=2,3,4,5$, and observing that the extra fraction is between zero and one for $t\ge6$, leaves only $t=2$.

Finally suppose one absolute value is at most one, and by symmetry take $n=0,1,-1$. For $n=0$, integrality of the second fraction $1/m$ gives $m=\pm1$. For $n=1$, the nonzero denominators allow cancellation to $1/(m-1)$, giving $m=0,2$. For $n=-1$, the second fraction is $(m+1)/(m^2+1)$; its only possibilities compatible with the other denominator are $m=-1,0$. Including swaps yields the finite list above. Direct substitution verifies every listed pair.

statement: Prove that every ten consecutive positive integers contain five that are pairwise coprime.
solution:
Among the five odd numbers, at most two are divisible by three. Discard one multiple of three, leaving four odd numbers with at most one multiple of three. No two of these four can share a prime factor greater than three: two odd multiples of five differ by at least ten, and two odd multiples of seven differ by at least fourteen.

statement: A convex cyclic octagon $A_1A_2\cdots A_8$ has alternate vertices $A_1,A_3,A_5,A_7$ forming a square of area $5$, while $A_2,A_4,A_6,A_8$ form a rectangle of area $4$. Find the maximum possible area of the octagon.
solution:
The maximum is $3\sqrt5$. Let the common circumradius be $R$, so $2R^2=5$. Choose the square's vertex angles as $0,\pi/2,\pi,3\pi/2$. The rectangle's angles are $a,b,a+\pi,b+\pi$, where $0<a<\pi/2<b<\pi$. Put $\delta=b-a$. The rectangle area condition is
$$2R^2\sin\delta=4,\qquad\sin\delta=4/5.$$
Summing the eight central triangle areas gives the octagon area
$$R^2(\sin a+\cos a+\sin b-\cos b)
=2\sqrt2R^2\sin\frac{a+b}{2}\cos\left(\frac\pi4-\frac\delta2\right).$$
The squared cosine factor is $(1+\sin\delta)/2=9/10$, and the sine factor is at most one. Therefore the area is at most $3\sqrt5$.

Equality is attainable: choose $a=(\pi-\delta)/2$ and $b=(\pi+\delta)/2$, where either angle $0<\delta<\pi$ satisfying $\sin\delta=4/5$ may be used. This preserves the alternating vertex order and makes $a+b=\pi$.
ratingReason: Both inscribed quadrilaterals must be parametrized on a common circle; summing central triangle areas exposes the independent rotation parameter to optimize.

statement: In acute triangle $ABC$, altitudes $AD,BE$ meet at $H$, and $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$. Circles $DEM$ and $ABH$ meet at $P,Q$, with $P$ on the same side of line $CH$ as $A$. Set $R=DE\cap PH$. Prove: (a) $\angle RDA=\angle RPA$ and $B,P,R,E$ are cyclic; (b) $R$ lies on circle $ABC$; (c) $DE,PH,MQ$ concur at $R$.
solution:
Use directed angles and let $F$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$. Since $A,B,D,E$ lie on the circle with diameter $AB$ and $A,B,H,P$ are cyclic,
$$\angle RDA=\angle EDA=\angle EBA=\angle HBA=\angle HPA=\angle RPA.$$
Thus $A,D,P,R$ are cyclic. It follows that
$$\angle PBE=\angle PBH=\angle PAH=\angle PAD=\angle PRD=\angle PRE,$$
so $B,E,P,R$ are cyclic as well.

The points $D,E,F,M,P$ lie on the nine-point circle of $ABC$. Using the two newly established circles gives
$$\angle ARB=\angle ARP+\angle PRB=\angle ADP+\angle PEB.$$
Split the last two angles through $F$. Their terms $\angle FDP$ and $\angle PEF$ cancel, because $D,E,F,P$ are cyclic. The remainder is
$$\angle ADF+\angle FEB=\angle ACF+\angle FCB=\angle ACB,$$
using circles $ACDF$ and $BCEF$. Hence $A,B,C,R$ are cyclic.

For the concurrence, invert about $M$ with radius $MA=MB=MD=ME$. Circle $DEM$, which passes through $M$, maps to line $DE$. Circle $ABH$ maps to circle $ABC$: these circles have equal radius $AB/(2\sin\angle ACB)$, share $A,B$, and have centres reflected in $M$; an inversion with the stated radius interchanges them.

Therefore the images $P',Q'$ are precisely the two intersections of $DE$ with circle $ABC$. One is $R$ by part (b). The image $P'$ lies on $MP$, whereas $R$ lies on $HP$, so it is the other intersection (the two lines meet at $P$, which is not on $DE$). Hence $R=Q'$, which lies on $MQ$. This proves the final concurrence.
ratingReason: The scaffold still requires several connected cyclicity arguments and an inversion that exchanges the altitude circle with the circumcircle.

statement: Circle $\Gamma_1$ is internally tangent to circle $\Gamma_2$ at $A$. From $P\in\Gamma_2$, $P\ne A$, draw tangents to $\Gamma_1$ touching at $B,C$. Lines $PB,PC$ meet $\Gamma_2$ again at $Q,R$. Prove $\angle QAR=2\angle BAC$. If line $BC$ meets $\Gamma_2$ at $E,F$ and $PE=PF$, prove $B,C,Q,R$ are cyclic.
solution:
For the first claim, combine the inscribed-angle theorem on the outer circle with the tangent-chord theorem on the inner one. In directed-angle form,
$$\angle QAR=\angle QPR=\angle QBC+\angle BCR=\angle BAC+\angle BAC.$$
The specified configuration gives the stated ordinary-angle equality.

For the second claim, let $O_1,O_2$ be the two centres. Equal tangents $PB=PC$ put $P,O_1$ on the perpendicular bisector of $BC$. The assumption $PE=PF$ puts $P,O_2$ on the perpendicular bisector of $EF$, which is the same line because $B,C,E,F$ are collinear. Thus $P,O_1,O_2$ lie on one line.

Reflection in this line preserves both circles, swaps $B,C$, and swaps $Q,R$. Hence $BC$ and $QR$ are parallel and the other two sides of quadrilateral $BCRQ$ are equal. It is an isosceles trapezoid, so it is cyclic. This is the required cyclicity of the four points.
ratingReason: The angle part combines the two circle configurations; the additional equal-distance condition must then be recognized as forcing a common symmetry axis.

statement: Call a permutation $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ of $1,\ldots,n$ square if every $a_i a_{i+1}+1$ is a perfect square. Construct square permutations for infinitely many $n$. Show that no permutation of $1,\ldots,n$, for any $n\ge2$, can instead make all these expressions perfect cubes.
solution:
For every odd integer $k\ge3$, take $n=k^2-1$ and use
$$2,4,6,\ldots,n,1,3,5,\ldots,n-1.$$
Within each parity block, successive terms differ by two, and $a(a+2)+1=(a+1)^2$. At the join, $n\cdot1+1=k^2$. This gives infinitely many square permutations.

For the cubic condition, let $a=2^k$ be the largest power of2 not exceeding $n$, so $a\le n<2a$ and $a\ge2$. It must have some neighbour $b$ in the permutation. If $ab+1=t^3$, then $t$ is odd and
$$ab=(t-1)(t^2+t+1).$$
The second factor is odd, so $a\mid t-1$, giving $t\ge a+1$. Therefore
$$b\ge\frac{(a+1)^3-1}{a}=a^2+3a+3>n,$$
a contradiction.
ratingReason: A parity-block construction gives infinitely many square cases; choosing the largest power of2 creates the cubic obstruction via a sharp size bound.
notes: Official ATSM paper; English paraphrase and independently written proof.

statement: Let $ABCD$ be a square. Choose $N\in AB$ and $P\in AD$ so that $PN=NC$, then choose $Q\in AN$ satisfying $\angle NCB=\angle QPN$. In a nondegenerate configuration, prove that $\angle BCQ=\tfrac12\angle PQA$.
solution:
Scale the square to $A=(0,0),B=(1,0),C=(1,1),D=(0,1)$, and write $P=(0,p),N=(n,0),Q=(q,0)$. The distance condition gives
$$n^2+p^2=(1-n)^2+1,\qquad n=1-\frac{p^2}{2}.$$
The equal-angle condition, using their tangents, becomes
$$1-n=\frac{p(n-q)}{p^2+nq}.$$
Substituting for $n$ and solving yields
$$q=\frac{2n-p^3}{2+pn}=\frac{2(1-p)}{2-p}.$$
The endpoint cases make one of the stated angles degenerate; thus $0<p<1$ and $0<q<1$.

Put $\theta=\angle BCQ$. Then $\tan\theta=1-q=p/(2-p)$, so $0<\theta<45^\circ$ and
$$\tan(2\theta)=\frac{2(1-q)}{1-(1-q)^2}=\frac pq=\tan\angle PQA.$$
Both doubled and target angles lie between $0$ and $90^\circ$, proving the equality.
ratingReason: The equal-distance condition controls the free parameter, and the second angle condition must be converted and simplified before a double-angle identity closes the proof.
notes: Official ATSM paper; English paraphrase and independently written proof.

statement: Two circles meet at $M,N$. Their common external tangent nearer to $M$ touches them at $A,B$. The line through $M$ parallel to $AB$ meets the circles again at $C,D$, respectively. Let $E=CA\cap DB$, $P=AN\cap CD$ and $Q=BN\cap CD$. Prove that $MN$ passes through the midpoint of $AB$ and that $EP=EQ$.
solution:
Let $I=MN\cap AB$. As $MN$ is the radical axis, $IA^2=IB^2$ by the tangent form of power of a point, so $I$ is the midpoint of $AB$. The homothety centred at $N$ taking line $AB$ to its parallel $CD$ sends $A,B,I$ to $P,Q,M$. Hence $M$ is the midpoint of $PQ$.

It remains to show $EM\perp CD$. Use coordinates with $AB$ horizontal: $A=(a,0),B=(b,0),M=(m,h)$. Each circle's centre lies vertically above or below its tangency point. Therefore its horizontal chord through $M$ has that vertical line as perpendicular bisector, giving
$$C=(2a-m,h),\qquad D=(2b-m,h).$$
The point $(m,-h)$ lies on both $AC$ and $BD$, so it is $E$. Thus $EM$ is vertical, while $PQ$ is horizontal. Since $M$ is its midpoint, $E$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $PQ$, proving $EP=EQ$.
ratingReason: The radical-axis midpoint must be transported to a second line; recognizing the reflected intersection then supplies the perpendicular bisector.
notes: Official ATSM paper; English paraphrase and independently written proof.

statement: In acute triangle $ABC$, let $D$ be the second intersection of the internal bisector of $\angle BAC$ with its circumcircle. Choose $E$ on ray $DC$ so that circle $ACE$ meets segment $BC$ again at $F$. Line $DF$ meets circle $ABC$ again at $G$, and circle $ACF$ again at $H$. Prove that $GC\parallel HE$.
solution:
Since $D$ is the midpoint of arc $BC$ not containing $A$, $DB=DC$. The cyclic angles give
$$\angle DGC=\angle DBC=\angle DCB=\angle DCF,$$
while $\angle GDC=\angle CDF$. Thus triangles $DGC$ and $DCF$ are similar, yielding
$$DF\cdot DG=DC^2.$$
The circle through $A,C,E,F$ gives, by power of $D$,
$$DF\cdot DH=DC\cdot DE.$$
Dividing the two identities gives $DH/DG=DE/DC$. As $D,H,G$ and $D,E,C$ are collinear, the converse of the intercept theorem gives $HE\parallel GC$. Directed lengths cover the possible orders on the rays.
ratingReason: The decisive step is an isosceles arc-midpoint similarity; comparing its product identity with a second circle power produces the required homothety.

statement: Find all positive integers $a,b$ for which $ab$ is a perfect square and $a^2+ab+b^2=p^k$ for some prime $p$ and positive integer $k$.
solution:
Exactly $a=b=3^t$ for integers $t\ge0$ work, with $p=3,k=2t+1$.

Put $d=\gcd(a,b)$. Since $ab$ is square and the quotients are coprime, write $a=du^2,b=dv^2$ with coprime positive integers $u,v$. Then
$$p^k=d^2(u^2+uv+v^2)(u^2-uv+v^2).$$
The two last factors are odd, and any common divisor divides $2uv$. Each is coprime to $uv$, so their gcd is1. Because their product is a prime power, the smaller factor must equal1. But
$$u^2-uv+v^2=(u-v)^2+uv\ge1,$$
with equality only at $u=v=1$. Hence $a=b=d$ and $3d^2=p^k$, forcing $p=3,d=3^t$. Direct substitution verifies all these pairs.
ratingReason: One must exploit the square product before factoring a quartic; coprimality of the two quadratic factors forces equality of the original variables.

statement:
Find every surjective function $f:\mathbb Q\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb Q\setminus\{0\}$ satisfying
$$(f(x)+f(y))f(x+y)=f(xy)$$
whenever $x,y$ and $x+y$ are nonzero rationals.
solution:
The unique solution is $f(x)=1/x$.

For any $x$, surjectivity provides $y$ with $f(y)=-f(x)$. If $x+y\ne0$, the displayed equation has zero left side and nonzero right side. Thus $y=-x$, proving oddness. The same argument shows injectivity: if $f(u)=f(v)$, then $f(u)+f(-v)=0$ forces $u=v$.

Taking $x=y=1$ gives $f(2)=1/2$, so $f(-2)=-1/2$. Write $c=f(1)$. The pair $(1,-2)$ gives
$$(c-1/2)(-c)=-1/2,$$
so $c=1$ or $-1/2$. The latter would make $f(1)+f(2)=0$ despite $1+2\ne0$, impossible. Thus $f(1)=1$.

Set $h(x)=1/f(x)$. It is odd and injective, and using the pair $(1,x)$ gives
$$h(x+1)=h(x)+1\qquad(x\ne0,-1).$$
Hence $h(n)=n$ for every nonzero integer, and repeated translation gives $h(x+n)=h(x)+n$ for nonintegral rational $x$ and positive integer $n$.

Rewriting the original equation with $y=n$ now gives
$$h(x)+n=\frac{(h(x)+n)h(nx)}{n h(x)}.$$
The factor $h(x)+n$ is nonzero: otherwise injectivity and $h(-n)=-n$ would imply $x=-n$. Therefore $h(nx)=nh(x)$. For $x=a/b$ with positive integer $b$ and nonzero integer $a$, take $n=b$ to obtain $h(x)=a/b=x$. The integral cases were already settled. Thus $f(x)=1/x$, which satisfies the equation and is surjective.
ratingReason: Surjectivity first forces both oddness and injectivity; reciprocal substitution then turns the equation into integer translations and rational homogeneity.

statement: Find all nonnegative integers $x,y$ and primes $p$ such that $x^2=p-2$ and $y^2=2p^2-2$.
solution:
The only triple is $(x,y,p)=(1,4,3)$.

If $p=2$, then $x=0$ but $y^2=6$, impossible. Thus $p$ is odd and $x$ is odd. Substituting $p=x^2+2$ gives
$$y^2=2(x^2+1)(x^2+3).$$
Write $a=(x^2+1)/2$ and $b=(x^2+3)/4$. Both are positive odd integers, since $x^2\equiv1\pmod8$, and $2b-a=1$, so $\gcd(a,b)=1$. The equation is $y^2=16ab$, hence $ab$ is square. Coprimality makes each factor square, say $b=v^2$.

Consequently $x^2+3=4v^2$, or
$$(2v-x)(2v+x)=3.$$
Both factors are positive integers, so they are1 and3. This yields $x=1,v=1$, then $p=3,y=4$, which indeed satisfy the equations.
ratingReason: Substitution exposes two near-consecutive factors, but parity and their exact gcd are needed before a square factor collapses the equation.

statement: In triangle $ABC$, the altitude feet from $A,B,C$ are $D,E,F$, and the orthocentre $H$ is the midpoint of $CF$. Let $M,N$ be the midpoints of $BC,BE$, respectively, and let $X=AN\cap MF$. Prove that $HX\perp XM$.
solution:
Take $A=(0,0),B=(b,0),C=(c,h)$ with $b,h>0$. Then $F=(c,0)$ and $H=(c,h/2)$. Since $BH\perp AC$,
$$h^2=2c(b-c).$$
Projecting $B$ onto $AC$ gives
$$E=\left(\frac{bc^2}{c^2+h^2},\frac{bch}{c^2+h^2}\right).$$
Using $c^2+h^2=c(2b-c)$, the midpoint $N$ has coordinates
$$N=\left(\frac{b^2}{2b-c},\frac{bh}{2(2b-c)}\right).$$
Thus $AN$ has slope $h/(2b)$, while $MF$ has slope $h/(b-c)$. Their intersection is
$$X=\left(\frac{2bc}{b+c},\frac{ch}{b+c}\right).$$
Now $X-H$ is a scalar multiple of $(c,-h/2)$, and a direction vector of $MF$ is $(b-c,h)$. Their dot product is $c(b-c)-h^2/2=0$. Therefore $HX\perp MF$, as required.
ratingReason: The midpoint condition on the orthocentre supplies a non-obvious metric relation; projecting an altitude foot then makes the two midpoint lines computable.

statement: Find all triples of distinct integers $x,y,z>1$ for which $z\mid xy-1$, $x\mid yz-1$ and $y\mid xz-1$.
solution:
The triples are the six permutations of $(2,3,5)$.

Each pair of variables is coprime: a common divisor of $x,y$, for example, would divide both $yz$ and $yz-1$. The integer $xy+xz+yz-1$ is divisible by each of $x,y,z$, and hence by their product. Therefore
$$K=\frac1x+\frac1y+\frac1z-\frac1{xyz}$$
is an integer. Assume $2\le x<y<z$. Clearly $K>0$, and $K<1/2+1/3+1/4<2$, so $K=1$. If $x\ge3$, then $K<1/3+1/4+1/5<1$, impossible. Thus $x=2$.

The equation $K=1$ becomes $2y+2z+yz-1=2yz$, or $(y-2)(z-2)=3$. With $y<z$ this gives $y=3,z=5$. The three divisibilities are immediate for these values.
ratingReason: Pairwise coprimality allows the three congruences to be combined into one small positive integer; an ordering bound then reduces the classification to a factorization.

statement:
Prove that the product
$$\prod_{r=2}^{22}\frac{r^6-1}{r^2-1}$$
is a perfect square.
solution:
Factor each quotient as
$$\frac{r^6-1}{r^2-1}=r^4+r^2+1=(r^2+r+1)(r^2-r+1).$$
The second factor equals $(r-1)^2+(r-1)+1$. Thus every intermediate factor occurs twice, leaving
$$\prod_{r=2}^{22}\frac{r^6-1}{r^2-1}
=3(22^2+22+1)\left(\prod_{r=2}^{21}(r^2+r+1)\right)^2.$$
Since $3(22^2+22+1)=3\cdot507=39^2$, the original product is the square of $39\prod_{r=2}^{21}(r^2+r+1)$.
ratingReason: A quartic factorization must be combined with a shifted index; the deliberately chosen endpoint makes the two unpaired factors a square.

statement: Independently colour each cell of a $3\times4$ rectangular grid red or green, with both colours equally likely. Find the probability that no $2\times2$ block is entirely green.
solution:
There are $2^{12}=4096$ equally likely colourings. Encode each column by a three-bit mask, with1 meaning green. Two successive masks are compatible exactly when their intersection does not contain two consecutive1s.

Among the eight masks, five ($000,001,010,100,101$) contain no consecutive1s; each can follow any mask. The masks $011,110$ each forbid itself and $111$ as the previous mask. Mask $111$ forbids $011,110,111$.

Let $a_j$ be the number of valid $j$-column grids ending in any one specified mask of the first group, $b_j$ the corresponding number for either of $011,110$, and $c_j$ the number ending in $111$. Symmetry and the compatibility rules give
$$a_{j+1}=5a_j+2b_j+c_j,\quad b_{j+1}=5a_j+b_j,\quad c_{j+1}=5a_j.$$
Starting with $(a_1,b_1,c_1)=(1,1,1)$ gives successively
$$(8,6,5),\qquad(57,46,40),\qquad(417,331,285).$$
Hence there are $5\cdot417+2\cdot331+285=3032$ permitted grids, and the probability is
$$\frac{3032}{4096}=\frac{379}{512}.$$
ratingReason: The overlapping forbidden blocks prevent independent-event counting; reducing column patterns to three state classes gives a compact exact enumeration.

statement: Prove that every prime congruent to $1$ modulo $4$ is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with positive integer side lengths.
solution:
Let $p\equiv1\pmod4$. We first prove $p=u^2+v^2$ with positive integers $u,v$.

Pairing each nonzero residue modulo $p$ with its multiplicative inverse proves Wilson's congruence $(p-1)!\equiv-1\pmod p$. Pairing instead $j$ with $p-j$, for $1\le j\le(p-1)/2$, shows that
$$r=\left(\frac{p-1}{2}\right)!\quad\text{satisfies}\quad r^2\equiv-1\pmod p,$$
because $(p-1)/2$ is even.

Put $m=\lfloor\sqrt p\rfloor$. Among the $(m+1)^2>p$ residues $a+rb$ with $0\le a,b\le m$, two coincide. Their differences $u,v$ are not both zero, satisfy $|u|,|v|\le m$, and obey $u+rv\equiv0\pmod p$. Hence $p\mid u^2+v^2$. But
$$0<u^2+v^2\le2m^2<2p,$$
so $u^2+v^2=p$. Neither coordinate is zero, since $p$ is not square; replace each by its absolute value.

Finally,
$$(u^2-v^2)^2+(2uv)^2=(u^2+v^2)^2=p^2.$$
The two legs $|u^2-v^2|$ and $2uv$ are positive integers, since $u=v$ would make the odd prime $p=2u^2$.
ratingReason: The result requires a substantive sum-of-two-squares lemma; a modular square root of−1 and a lattice-style pigeonhole argument construct it before the Pythagorean identity.

statement: Three circles $\Omega_a,\Omega_b,\Omega_c$ are pairwise externally tangent at $D\in\Omega_a\cap\Omega_b$, $E\in\Omega_b\cap\Omega_c$ and $F\in\Omega_c\cap\Omega_a$. Start with $P\in\Omega_a$ distinct from $D,F$. Extend $PD$ to meet $\Omega_b$ again at $B$, extend $BE$ to meet $\Omega_c$ again at $C$, and extend $CF$ to meet $\Omega_a$ again at $A$. Prove that $PA$ is a diameter of $\Omega_a$.
solution:
Let the circle radii be $r_a,r_b,r_c$. The homothety centred at the external tangency point $D$, with ratio $-r_b/r_a$, takes $\Omega_a$ to $\Omega_b$ and therefore takes $P$ to $B$. Similarly, the homotheties centred at $E,F$, with respective ratios $-r_c/r_b$ and $-r_a/r_c$, take $B$ to $C$ and $C$ to $A$.

Their composition has ratio
$$\left(-\frac{r_b}{r_a}\right)\left(-\frac{r_c}{r_b}\right)\left(-\frac{r_a}{r_c}\right)=-1.$$
A composition of homotheties with ratio $-1$ is a half-turn. It takes $\Omega_a$ onto itself, so its centre is the centre of $\Omega_a$. Thus it takes every point to its antipode, and in particular $P,A$ are the endpoints of a diameter.
ratingReason: Recognizing the three successive chord constructions as negative homotheties turns a complicated-looking diagram into a composition with ratio−1.

statement:
For positive real numbers $a,b,c$ with $abc=1$, prove
$$\frac{1+a+ab}{1+b+ab}+\frac{1+b+bc}{1+c+bc}+\frac{1+c+ca}{1+a+ca}\ge3.$$
solution:
Write $a=x/y,b=y/z,c=z/x$ with positive $x,y,z$. The three numerators become the common symmetric expression $xy+yz+zx$, divided respectively by $yz,zx,xy$. The denominators reduce to $(x+y+z)/z$, $(x+y+z)/x$, $(x+y+z)/y$.

Consequently the original sum equals
$$\frac{xy+yz+zx}{x+y+z}\left(\frac1x+\frac1y+\frac1z\right)
=\frac{(xy+yz+zx)^2}{xyz(x+y+z)}.$$
Set $u=xy,v=yz,w=zx$. The needed bound is $(u+v+w)^2\ge3(uv+vw+wu)$, which follows from
$$u^2+v^2+w^2-uv-vw-wu=\frac12\bigl((u-v)^2+(v-w)^2+(w-u)^2\bigr)\ge0.$$
Equality holds when $x=y=z$, or $a=b=c=1$.
ratingReason: The product constraint suggests a cyclic ratio substitution; after that the asymmetric fractions unexpectedly combine into one symmetric square.
notes: National Mathematical Centre original paper, publicly mirrored by Special Maths Academy; scan visually checked including cover date. Independently written mathematical paraphrase and proof.

statement: Let $D$ lie inside triangle $ABC$. Put $E=BD\cap AC$, $F=CD\cap AB$ and $G=EF\cap BC$. Choose $H$ on line $AD$, and set $I=HF\cap BD$, $J=HE\cap CD$. Prove that $G,I,J$ are collinear whenever the named intersections form a nondegenerate configuration.
solution:
Apply the converse of Desargues' theorem to triangles $BIF$ and $CJE$, with corresponding vertices $B\leftrightarrow C$, $I\leftrightarrow J$, $F\leftrightarrow E$. The corresponding sides meet at
$$BI\cap CJ=D,\qquad BF\cap CE=A,\qquad IF\cap JE=H.$$
These points are collinear, so the three joining lines $BC,IJ,FE$ concur. The first and third meet at $G$, proving the claim.

Here is a coordinate verification that does not assume the theorem. Use homogeneous barycentric coordinates, rescaled so that
$$A=(1:0:0),\ B=(0:1:0),\ C=(0:0:1),\ D=(1:1:1).$$
Such a rescaling is possible because $D$ is interior and all three barycentric coordinates are nonzero. Then
$$E=(1:0:1),\ F=(1:1:0),\ G=(0:1:-1),\ H=(h:k:k).$$
The equation of $HF$ is $-kX+kY+(h-k)Z=0$, while $BD$ has $X=Z$. Hence $I=(k:2k-h:k)$. Interchanging the last two coordinates gives $J=(k:k:2k-h)$. Their representing vectors differ by a multiple of $(0,1,-1)$, so $G,I,J$ are collinear.
ratingReason: The construction hides two triangles whose corresponding side intersections lie on AD; finding that correspondence or constructing a suitable homogeneous coordinate system is the main difficulty.

statement: For an integer $N\ge2$, prove that $4n(N-n)+1$ is never a perfect square for any integer $1\le n<N$ if and only if $N^2+1$ is prime.
solution:
First suppose $N$ is odd. Then $N^2+1$ is composite, and $n=(N-1)/2$ makes $4n(N-n)+1=N^2$, so both sides of the equivalence are false. We may assume $N$ is even.

We use the following elementary lemma: every prime $p\equiv1\pmod4$ has a representation $p=r^2+s^2$ with positive integers $r,s$. To prove it, Wilson's theorem gives a residue $w$ with $w^2\equiv-1\pmod p$: take $w=((p-1)/2)!$. Among the $(m+1)^2>p$ numbers $a+wb$ with $0\le a,b\le m=\lfloor\sqrt p\rfloor$, two are congruent. Their nonzero difference pair has squared norm divisible by $p$, positive and less than $2p$, so the norm is $p$.

Suppose first that $P=N^2+1$ is prime and that some $4n(N-n)+1=b^2$. Put $a=N-2n$. Then
$$a^2+b^2=P,\qquad |a|<N.$$
Modulo $P$, the identity $(Na-b)(Na+b)\equiv-(a^2+b^2)\equiv0$ lets us choose the sign of $b$ so that $P\mid Na+b$. It also follows that $P\mid Nb-a$. The exact identity
$$(Na+b)^2+(Nb-a)^2=P^2$$
therefore forces one of these two multiples of $P$ to be zero and the other to be $\pm P$. Solving gives only $(a,b)=(\pm N,\pm1)$ or $(\pm1,\pm N)$, with the appropriate signs. The first alternatives violate $|a|<N$; the second violate the fact that $a=N-2n$ is even. Thus no such square occurs.

Conversely, suppose $N^2+1$ is composite and let $p$ be its smallest prime factor. Then $p\le\sqrt{N^2+1}<N+1$, so $p\le N$. Since $N^2\equiv-1\pmod p$, the prime $p$ is $1$ modulo4: Fermat's theorem rules out $p\equiv3\pmod4$, and $p$ is odd. By the lemma write $p=r^2+s^2$, choosing positive $r,s$ with their order such that $Nr\equiv-s\pmod p$. This order is available: if $Nr\equiv s$, interchanging $r,s$ changes the sign of the corresponding ratio, because $(s/r)(r/s)=1$ and $(s/r)^2\equiv-1$.

The numbers
$$u=\frac{Nr+s}{p},\qquad v=\frac{r-Ns}{p}$$
are integers and satisfy
$$N=ru-sv,\qquad1=su+rv.$$
Moreover $u>Nr/p\ge r$, so $u\ge2$, while $v<0$. Now put
$$a=ru+sv,\qquad b=rv-su=1-2su.$$
Then $a^2+b^2=(r^2+s^2)(u^2+v^2)=N^2+1$. Also $|b|\ge3$, and $a$ is even, as seen from
$$a=\frac{N(r^2-s^2)+2rs}{p}.$$
We cannot have $a=0$, since $N^2+1$ is not a square; hence $0<|a|<N$. Taking $n=(N-|a|)/2$ gives an integer $1\le n<N$ and
$$4n(N-n)+1=N^2-a^2+1=b^2.$$
This completes both directions.
ratingReason: This is an upper-band problem: the square condition must be recast as a second sum-of-two-squares representation, and the composite direction needs a constructive factor-conjugation argument plus the prime representation lemma.

competition: Moroccan National Olympiad Programme — National Camp Contest
statement: Let $ABC$ be acute with $AB<AC$. Let $D$ be the midpoint of $AC$, let $E$ be the foot of the altitude from $A$, and put $F=AB\cap DE$. On arc $BC$ of the circumcircle not containing $A$, choose $H$ with $\angle BHE=\angle ABC$. Prove that $BH\perp HF$.
solution:
Write the angles at $B,C$ as $\beta,\gamma$. Because $D$ is the midpoint of the hypotenuse of right triangle $AEC$, we have $DA=DC=DE$. Angle chasing in these isosceles triangles gives $\angle EFA=\beta-\gamma$. The given condition and the cyclic quadrilateral $ABHC$ give $\angle EHA=\beta-\gamma$ as well. Consequently $A,E,H,F$ are concyclic.

Now $\angle AHF=\angle AEF=90^\circ+\gamma$, while $\angle AHB=\gamma$. Subtracting gives $\angle BHF=90^\circ$. These equalities can equivalently be read as directed-angle equalities modulo $180^\circ$.
ratingReason: The midpoint of a right-triangle hypotenuse reveals a useful angle; a second, initially hidden cyclic quadrilateral completes the proof.

competition: Moroccan National Olympiad Programme — National Camp Contest
statement: Find all functions $f:\mathbb Q_{>0}\to\mathbb Q_{>0}$ for which some rational $\alpha>0$ satisfies $$f(x/y+y)=f(x)/f(y)+f(y)+\alpha x$$ for every positive rational $x,y$.
solution:
The solution is $f(x)=x^2$, with $\alpha=2$.

Replacing $x$ by $xy$ gives
$$f(x+y)=\frac{f(xy)}{f(y)}+f(y)+\alpha xy.\tag{1}$$
Put $c=f(1)$. Comparing (1) at $(x,1)$ and $(1,x)$ yields $(1-c)(f(x)-c)=0$. If $c\ne1$, $f$ is constant, impossible in the original equation as $x$ varies. Thus $c=1$, and induction gives $f(n)=n+\alpha n(n-1)/2$ for integers $n\ge1$. Also $f(t)>\alpha(t-1)$ for $t>1$.

To prove injectivity, suppose $f(a)=f(b)$ with $a>b$. The original equation gives
$$f(t)=f\left(\frac ab(t-a)+b\right)\qquad(t>a).$$
The affine map on the right has fixed point $a+b$ and slope $a/b>1$. Starting at $t_0=a+b+1$ and iterating therefore gives $t_m\to\infty$ with $f(t_m)=f(t_0)$, contradicting the preceding lower bound. Hence $f$ is injective.

Symmetry of (1) now gives $f(xy)=f(x)f(y)$ whenever $x\ne y$. In particular $f(6)=f(2)f(3)$ gives
$$6+15\alpha=(2+\alpha)(3+3\alpha),$$
so $\alpha=2$. Thus $f(n)=n^2$ on the positive integers. For a nonintegral rational $x=p/q$, multiplicativity with the integer $q\ne x$ gives $p^2=f(qx)=q^2f(x)$, proving $f(x)=x^2$ everywhere. Direct substitution verifies the result.
ratingReason: The main obstacle is proving injectivity without regularity; an expanding affine orbit and positivity supply it, after which multiplicativity determines the function.

competition: Moroccan National Olympiad Programme — National Camp Contest
statement: Find all composite integers $n>1$ such that every divisor $d>1$ of $n$ can be written $d=a^r+1$, where $a$ is a positive integer and $r>1$ is an integer.
solution:
The only answer is $n=10$.

First every divisor $d>1$ must be one more than a square. Indeed, write $d-1=b^s$ with the exponent $s$ maximal. If $b=1$ this is immediate. Otherwise $b$ is not itself a perfect power, and $s>1$. If $s$ were odd, $b+1$ would divide $d$ and hence $n$. Applying the hypothesis to $b+1$ would make $b$ a perfect power, a contradiction. Thus $s$ is even.

No prime square can divide $n$, since $p^2=x^2+1$ has no positive integer solution. Hence $n$ is squarefree. Choose distinct prime divisors $p>q$, and write $p=x^2+1$, $q=y^2+1$, $pq=z^2+1$. We have $x<z<p$, and
$$p\mid z^2-x^2=(z-x)(z+x).$$
Since $0<z-x<p$ and $0<z+x<2p$, primality forces $z+x=p$. Substitution gives
$$q=\frac{(p-x)^2+1}{p}=(x-1)^2+1.$$
The primes $x^2+1$ and $(x-1)^2+1$ have opposite parity. The smaller must therefore be2, giving $x=2$ and $\{p,q\}=\{5,2\}$. Every pair of distinct prime factors must be this pair, so squarefreeness and compositeness give $n=10$. Its nontrivial divisors are $2=1^2+1$, $5=2^2+1$, and $10=3^2+1$.
ratingReason: A maximal perfect-power representation first turns every exponent into an even one; squarefreeness and a sharp prime-divisibility interval then force the sole pair of prime factors.

competition: Moroccan National Olympiad Programme — National Camp Contest
statement: Find the least real constant $c>0$ such that $$\gcd\bigl(n,\lfloor n\sqrt2\rfloor\bigr)\le c\sqrt n$$ for every positive integer $n$.
solution:
The least constant is $2^{3/4}$.

Write $d=\gcd(n,\lfloor n\sqrt2\rfloor)$, $n=dr$, and $\lfloor n\sqrt2\rfloor=ds$. The floor inequalities give
$$d^2s^2<2d^2r^2<(ds+1)^2.$$
Since the middle and left expressions are integers, $k=2r^2-s^2$ is a positive integer and $d^2k\le2ds$, hence $d\le2s/k\le2s<2\sqrt2\,r$. Therefore $d^2<2\sqrt2\,dr=2\sqrt2\,n$.

For sharpness, take the unbounded positive solutions $(s,r)$ of $s^2-2r^2=-1$, generated by
$$s+r\sqrt2=(1+\sqrt2)(3+2\sqrt2)^m.$$
Set $n=2sr$. We have
$$2s^2<n\sqrt2<2s^2+1,$$
because the squares of the latter two bounds differ from $2n^2$ by $4s^2$ and1 respectively. Thus $\lfloor n\sqrt2\rfloor=2s^2$. The Pell equation implies $\gcd(s,r)=1$, so the gcd is $2s$. Its ratio to $\sqrt n$ equals $\sqrt{2s/r}$, tending to $2^{3/4}$. No smaller constant works.
ratingReason: Reparametrizing by the gcd gives the upper bound, but proving optimality requires constructing a Pell sequence and checking the floor and gcd exactly.

competition: Moroccan National Olympiad Programme — National Camp Contest
statement: The positive integers are coloured with finitely many colours. Prove that there are four distinct positive integers $a,b,c,d$ of one colour such that $ad=bc$, $c/a=2024^n$, and $b/a=2025^m$ for some positive integers $n,m$.
solution:
Suppose there are $k$ colours, and colour the lattice point $(i,j)$ by the colour of $2024^i2025^j$.

We first find a monochromatic rectangle. Use $k+1$ fixed rows and more than $k^{k+1}$ columns. Two columns have identical colour vectors. In their common vector, two of the $k+1$ entries share a colour; those two rows and columns form the desired rectangle.

Write its coordinates as $i_1<i_2$ and $j_1<j_2$, and set
$$a=2024^{i_1}2025^{j_1},\quad b=2024^{i_1}2025^{j_2},\quad c=2024^{i_2}2025^{j_1},\quad d=2024^{i_2}2025^{j_2}.$$
The four values are distinct because2024 and2025 are coprime and both exceed1. They have one colour and satisfy the required equations with $n=i_2-i_1$ and $m=j_2-j_1$.
ratingReason: The multiplicative equations become a rectangular grid pattern; two nested pigeonhole arguments produce a monochromatic rectangle with all four entries distinct.

competition: Moroccan National Olympiad Programme — National Camp Contest
statement: Let $D$ and $E$ lie on the arcs $AB$ and $AC$ of the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ that avoid $C$ and $B$, respectively. Put $M=DE\cap AB$ and $N=DE\cap AC$. Suppose circles $BDN$ and $CEM$ meet at $X,Y$. Prove that $A,X,Y$ are collinear if and only if $DE\parallel BC$.
solution:
Let $B'$ be the second intersection of $AB$ with circle $BDN$, and $C'$ the second intersection of $AC$ with circle $CEM$. Use directed segments throughout.

Cyclic angles show $NB'\parallel AE$ and $MC'\parallel AD$. The corresponding similar triangles give
$$\frac{AB'}{MB'}=\frac{EN}{MN},\qquad \frac{AC'}{NC'}=\frac{DM}{MN}.$$
Taking their quotient and then using the powers of $M$ and $N$ with respect to the two small circles yields
$$\frac{AB'}{AC'}=\frac{MB'\,EN}{NC'\,DM}
=\frac{(MD\,MN/MB)\,EN}{(NE\,NM/NC)\,DM}=\frac{NC}{MB}.$$
Now $A$ lies on the common radical axis $XY$ exactly when
$$AB\cdot AB'=AC\cdot AC',$$
or $AB'/AC'=AC/AB$. Combining the ratio identity gives $NC/AC=MB/AB$, which is precisely the intercept-theorem condition for $MN\parallel BC$.
ratingReason: Two auxiliary second intersections turn the common radical-axis condition into a length ratio; deriving that ratio requires both parallelisms and two circle powers.

competition: Moroccan National Olympiad Programme — National Camp Contest
statement: A nonconstant real polynomial $f$ satisfies $$\frac{f(n+1)\cdots f(n+k)}{f(1)\cdots f(k)}\in\mathbb Z$$ for all positive integers $n,k$; in particular all the denominators are nonzero. Prove that $f(0)=0$.
solution:
Multiplying $f$ by any nonzero constant leaves the hypothesis unchanged. Normalize $f(1)=1$. The case $k=1$ shows that $f$ takes integer values at every positive integer. Interpolation at $\deg f+1$ positive integers therefore gives rational coefficients. Clearing denominators, we may assume $f\in\mathbb Z[x]$.

Fix $k\ge1$ and put $g(x)=\prod_{j=1}^k f(x+j)$ and $M=g(0)\ne0$. The hypothesis says $M\mid g(n)$ for every positive integer $n$. Choose a positive $n\equiv-1\pmod{|M|}$. Since $g$ has integer coefficients, $g(-1)\equiv g(n)\equiv0\pmod M$. Hence
$$\frac{g(-1)}{M}=\frac{f(0)}{f(k)}\in\mathbb Z.$$
As $k\to\infty$, the nonconstant polynomial has $|f(k)|\to\infty$. The displayed integer tends to0, so it is eventually0; thus $f(0)=0$.
ratingReason: Normalization and interpolation recover integral coefficients; a negative input is then accessed through positive congruent inputs, forcing an integer quotient to tend to zero.

competition: Moroccan National Olympiad Programme — Team Selection Test
statement: Points $1,2,\ldots,n$, with $n\ge4$, occur consecutively on a circle. Two players alternately draw chords joining labels of the same parity. Drawn chords may neither cross nor share endpoints. The player who makes the last move wins. Determine which player has a winning strategy.
solution:
The second player wins exactly when $n\equiv2\pmod4$.

Only cyclic order matters, so arrange relevant points regularly whenever using a symmetry. For $n=4k+2$, the second player answers each chord by its half-turn image. This preserves the same-parity condition, and no legal chord is a diameter, since opposite labels have opposite parity. A chord and its half-turn image are disjoint. The paired position remains invariant, so the response always exists.

For $n=4k$, the first player begins with diameter $(1,2k+1)$, then answers by half-turn symmetry in the two separated semicircles.

For $n=4k+1$, the first player draws $(1,3)$, isolating point2. The remaining $4k-2$ points alternate in parity, and the first player can now act as the second player in the previous $4\ell+2$ strategy.

For $n=4k+3$, the first move is $(2k+1,2k+3)$, isolating $2k+2$. The other $4k$ points, in cyclic order, are $1,\ldots,2k,2k+4,\ldots,4k+3$. Pair corresponding points in these two blocks. Each pair has opposite parity, while the pairing reverses parity on every point. It therefore maps legal chords to legal chords and fixes none. Realize the remaining cyclic order as a regular $4k$-gon; the same half-turn response strategy wins.
ratingReason: The usual pairing strategy must be adapted to all four residue classes, including an odd case where deleting three points changes the parity pattern.

competition: Moroccan National Olympiad Programme — Team Selection Test
statement: In a triangle $ABC$ with $AB<AC$, let $I,O,R$ denote the incentre, circumcentre and circumradius. The external bisector of angle $A$ meets line $BC$ at $T$. Let $K$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ with $IK\perp IT$. Prove that $OK=3R$.
solution:
Scale to $B=(-1,0)$, $C=(1,0)$, and write $A=(u,v)$ with $v>0$. Put $b=AC$, $c=AB$, $q=b+c$, and $d=b-c>0$. The distance equations give
$$u=-\frac{dq}{4},\qquad 16v^2=(q^2-4)(4-d^2).$$
The standard weighted-coordinate formula for the incentre, and the external angle-bisector theorem, give
$$I=\left(-\frac d2,\frac{2v}{q+2}\right),\qquad T=\left(-\frac qd,0\right).$$
Write $I=(i,j)$ and $K=(0,k)$. The perpendicularity condition is
$$(-i,k-j)\mathbin\cdot(-q/d-i,-j)=0,$$
so
$$k=\frac{2v}{q+2}-\frac{(2q-d^2)(q+2)}{8v}.$$
Also $O=(0,o)$, where $o=(u^2+v^2-1)/(2v)=(q^2+d^2-8)/(8v)$. Substitution of the expression for $v^2$ simplifies the difference to
$$k-o=-\frac{3(q^2-d^2)}{8v}.$$
Finally the area of $ABC$ is $v$, so $R=BC\cdot AC\cdot AB/(4v)=bc/(2v)=(q^2-d^2)/(8v)$. Thus $|k-o|=3R$, proving the claim.
ratingReason: The metric constant is not apparent from the diagram; side-sum and side-difference coordinates synchronize the external bisector, incentre and circumcentre.

competition: Moroccan National Olympiad Programme — Team Selection Test
statement: Let $a_1,\ldots,a_k$ be positive integers and let $f\in\mathbb Z[x]$ be nonconstant. Prove that infinitely many primes $p$ divide $$f(n)+a_1^n+\cdots+a_k^n$$ for infinitely many positive integers $n$.
solution:
We first prove that a nonconstant integer polynomial $g$ has infinitely many prime divisors among its nonzero integer values. Suppose only primes in a finite set occur, and let $P$ be their product. Choose $t$ with $c=g(t)\ne0$. Then
$$h(m)=\frac{g(t+cPm)}{c}$$
is a nonconstant integer polynomial with $h(m)\equiv1\pmod P$. Choose $m$ with $|h(m)|>1$. A prime divisor of $h(m)$ divides a value of $g$, yet divides neither $P$ nor $c$, a contradiction.

Apply this lemma to $g(x)=f(x)+k$. Excluding the finitely many primes dividing $a_1\cdots a_k$ leaves infinitely many primes $p$, each with some integer $t$ satisfying $f(t)+k\equiv0\pmod p$.

For each such prime, the Chinese remainder theorem gives infinitely many positive $n$ with
$$n\equiv t\pmod p,\qquad n\equiv0\pmod{p-1}.$$
The polynomial values satisfy $f(n)\equiv f(t)\pmod p$, while Fermat's theorem gives $a_i^n\equiv1\pmod p$ for every $i$. Their sum is therefore divisible by $p$.
ratingReason: One must establish an infinite-prime-divisor lemma, remove the exponential bases’ bad primes, and synchronize polynomial and exponential residues by CRT.

competition: Moroccan National Olympiad Programme — Team Selection Test
statement: Determine all finite tuples $(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$ of pairwise distinct positive integers such that, for every $i,j$, some $k$ satisfies $$a_i\equiv-2a_k\pmod{a_j}.$$ The order of the tuple is immaterial.
solution:
The possibilities are a single positive integer $(t)$, or the two integers $(t,3t)$ in either order.

Divide all entries by their gcd; this preserves the condition. At least one normalized entry is odd. Fixing it as $a_i$, the condition says every $a_j$ divides an odd integer $a_i+2a_k$, so all entries are odd.

Order them as $a_1<\cdots<a_n=M$. For each $i<n$, choose $k$ with $M\mid a_i+2a_k$. We cannot have $k=n$, because then $M\mid a_i$. Hence the positive sum is less than $3M$. It is odd, so cannot be $2M$; therefore
$$a_i+2a_k=M.$$
The map $i\mapsto k$ is strictly decreasing and bijects $\{1,\ldots,n-1\}$ with itself. Thus $k=n-i$. Taking $i=1$ and $i=n-1$ gives
$$a_1+2a_{n-1}=M=a_{n-1}+2a_1,$$
forcing $a_1=a_{n-1}$. Consequently $n\le2$. In the two-entry case $M=3a_1$, and undoing the normalization gives $(t,3t)$. These tuples satisfy the condition directly.
ratingReason: Normalizing by the gcd forces parity, and the largest modulus turns a congruence into an exact identity; its order-reversing permutation leaves at most two entries.
