competition: Moroccan National Olympiad Programme — Team Selection Test
statement: Find every function $f:\mathbb R_{>0}\to\mathbb R_{>0}$ satisfying $$x+f(yf(x)+1)=xf(x+y)+yf(yf(x))$$ for all positive reals $x,y$.
solution:
The unique solution is $f(x)=1/x$.

We first prove injectivity. Suppose $f(u)=f(v)$ with $u>v>0$. Comparing the equations at $(u,y)$ and $(v,y)$, and writing $C=u-v$, gives
$$f(t+C)-1=\frac vu\bigl(f(t)-1\bigr)\qquad(t>v).$$
Thus, for any fixed $t>v$, the sequence $f(t+nC)$ tends to1. Let $a_n=t+nC$. Substituting $y=a_n/f(x)$ in the original equation, for any fixed $x>0$, yields
$$x+f(a_n+1)=xf\left(x+\frac{a_n}{f(x)}\right)+\frac{a_n}{f(x)}f(a_n).$$
The left side tends to $x+1$, while positivity makes the right side at least $a_nf(a_n)/f(x)\to\infty$. This contradiction proves injectivity; no continuity assumption was used.

Now substitute $y=x/f(x)$ into the original equation. Cancellation gives
$$f(x+1)=xf\left(x+\frac{x}{f(x)}\right).$$
Taking $x=1$ and using injectivity gives $f(1)=1$. The original equation with $x=1$ then reduces to $1=yf(y)$, so $f(y)=1/y$. Direct substitution checks this function.
ratingReason: Injectivity is hidden behind a nonlinear substitution; assuming a collision creates a geometric approach to1 along an arithmetic progression, which positivity contradicts.

title: A geometric sum that is a square
statement: Find all positive integer pairs $(x,y)$ satisfying $y^2(x-1)=x^5-1$.
solution: For $x=1$, every positive $y$ works. For $x>1$, put $F=x^4+x^3+x^2+x+1=y^2$. If $x$ is even, $F$ lies strictly between $(x^2+x/2)^2$ and $(x^2+x/2+1)^2$: the respective differences are $3x^2/4+x+1>0$ and $5x^2/4>0$. If $x$ is odd and $x>3$, it lies strictly between $(x^2+(x-1)/2)^2$ and $(x^2+(x+1)/2)^2$; the upper difference is $(x-3)(x+1)/4>0$, and the lower difference is positive. The only remaining value $x=3$ gives $y=11$. Thus the answers are $(1,y)$ for all positive $y$, and $(3,11)$.
ratingReason: The exceptional x=1 case must be separated; parity-sensitive consecutive-square bounds then isolate x=3.

title: A parallel through a cevian foot
statement: Concurrent cevians $AK,BL,CM$ of triangle $ABC$ meet the opposite sides at $K,L,M$. The line through $M$ parallel to $KL$ meets $BC$ at $V$ and $AK$ at $W$. Prove that $VM=MW$.
solution: Use affine coordinates $A=(0,1),B=(0,0),C=(1,0)$ and write $K=(k,0),L=(l,1-l),M=(0,m)$. Ceva gives $k(1-l)(1-m)=lm(1-k)$, hence $k(1-l-m+2lm)=lm$. The line through $M$ parallel to $KL$ has parametrisation $(t(l-k),m+t(1-l))$. Its intersection with $BC$ has parameter $-m/(1-l)$. At the opposite parameter $m/(1-l)$, the coordinates satisfy $x/k+y=1$ by the displayed Ceva identity, so this point is $W$. Thus $M$ is the midpoint of $VW$.
ratingReason: Ceva supplies a product of ratios, which must be translated through a parallel line into the required midpoint relation.

title: A functional equation with cube roots
statement: Determine all functions $f:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ such that $f(1)=1/2$ and $f(xy)=f(x)f(\sqrt[3]{y})+f(y)f(\sqrt[3]{x})$ for positive $x,y$.
solution: Setting $y=1$ gives $f(\sqrt[3]{x})=f(x)$. Thus $g=2f$ satisfies $g(xy)=g(x)g(y)$, $g(1)=1$, and $g(\sqrt[3]{x})=g(x)$. Therefore $g(x)^3=g(x)$. Also $g(x)g(1/x)=1$, so $g(x)\ne0$, while $g(x)=g(\sqrt{x})^2>0$. Hence $g(x)=1$ for every positive $x$. The unique solution is $f(x)=1/2$, which directly satisfies the equation.
ratingReason: The substitution y=1 yields cube-root invariance; combining it with multiplicativity and positivity excludes both zero and negative values.

title: An infinite family with a fixed sum of proper divisors
statement: Let $\sigma(n)$ be the sum of the positive divisors of $n$. Suppose a fixed positive integer $k$ and a strictly increasing infinite sequence $n_1,n_2,\ldots$ satisfy $\sigma(n_i)-n_i=k$. Prove that every $n_i$ is prime.
solution: If $n$ is composite, its smallest prime factor $p$ satisfies $p\le\sqrt n$. Thus $n/p$ is a proper divisor at least $\sqrt n$, giving $k=\sigma(n)-n\ge\sqrt n$ and $n\le k^2$. Only finitely many composite terms are therefore possible. Since the sequence is infinite, it contains a prime term, for which the sum of proper divisors is 1. Hence $k=1$. Every composite integer has at least the two proper divisors 1 and a prime factor, so its proper-divisor sum exceeds 1; also $\sigma(1)-1=0$. Consequently every term is prime.
ratingReason: A composite number has a proper divisor at least its square root, bounding every composite candidate by k²; infinitude then forces k=1.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

provenance.archive: University of Western Australia olympiad archive

title: An infinite monochromatic staircase
statement: Colour each lattice point $(x,y)$ with nonnegative integer coordinates red or blue. Prove that there is an infinite monochromatic sequence $(x_1,y_1),(x_1,y_2),(x_2,y_2),(x_2,y_3),\ldots$, with both coordinate sequences strictly increasing.
solution: If infinitely many horizontal lines have only finitely many blue points, select their heights increasingly. On each selected line all sufficiently far-right points are red; choose each next vertical segment beyond the thresholds for its two endpoint rows. This builds a red staircase. The same argument works after swapping colours or coordinates. Otherwise, each of these four exceptional-line families is finite. Beyond some coordinate threshold, every horizontal and vertical line contains infinitely many points of each colour. Begin at any point in that quadrant. Move upward to a point of the same colour, then rightward to another, and repeat. Each step can be made strictly positive and remains in the quadrant.
ratingReason: The infinite construction needs a dichotomy: infinitely many almost-monochromatic rows or columns, or a quadrant where both colours recur on every line.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

provenance.archive: University of Western Australia olympiad archive

title: The product of divisors determines the integer
statement: Write $P(n)$ for the product of all positive divisors of $n$. Prove that positive integers $a,b$ with $P(a)=P(b)$ must satisfy $a=b$.
solution: Let $d(n)$ be the number of divisors. Pairing complementary divisors gives $P(n)^2=n^{d(n)}$. Thus $a^{d(a)}=b^{d(b)}$. If either integer is 1, both are. Otherwise they have the same prime factors; write $a=\prod p_i^{\alpha_i}$ and $b=\prod p_i^{\beta_i}$. Equality implies $\alpha_i d(a)=\beta_i d(b)$ for every $i$. If $d(a)>d(b)$, then every $\alpha_i<\beta_i$, so $d(a)=\prod(\alpha_i+1)<\prod(\beta_i+1)=d(b)$, a contradiction. The reverse inequality is equally impossible. Therefore the divisor counts and all prime exponents agree.
ratingReason: The product-of-divisors formula turns equality into proportional prime-exponent vectors; the divisor counts then force the opposite ordering unless the vectors coincide.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

provenance.archive: University of Western Australia olympiad archive

title: Two cevians and the altitude
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $\angle ABC=60^\circ$ and $\angle BAC=40^\circ$. Choose $P\in AB$ with $\angle BCP=70^\circ$ and $Q\in AC$ with $\angle CBQ=40^\circ$. If $R=CP\cap BQ$, prove that $AR\perp BC$.
solution: Let $H$ be the foot of the altitude from $A$. Since $\angle C=80^\circ$, we have $\angle BAH=30^\circ$, $\angle HAC=10^\circ$, $\angle QBA=20^\circ$, and $\angle ACP=10^\circ$. The trigonometric Ceva product for $AH,BQ,CP$ is $\frac{\sin30^\circ}{\sin10^\circ}\frac{\sin40^\circ}{\sin20^\circ}\frac{\sin10^\circ}{\sin70^\circ}=1$, using $\sin40^\circ=2\sin20^\circ\cos20^\circ$ and $\sin70^\circ=\cos20^\circ$. Thus the three cevians concur, so $R\in AH$.
ratingReason: Trigonometric Ceva recognises the altitude as the third cevian; the required product collapses using a double-angle identity.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

provenance.archive: University of Western Australia olympiad archive

title: A rectangle among four tangent-circle centres
statement: A semicircle with centre $O$ has diameter $AB$. A circle with centre $P$ touches the semicircle and touches $AB$ at $O$. A second semicircle has centre $Q$ on $AB$ and is tangent to the first semicircle and the circle centred at $P$. A circle centred at $R$ lies inside the first semicircle and touches it internally and the other two curves externally. Prove that $OPRQ$ is a rectangle.
solution: Scale the first radius to 1 and take $O=(0,0)$, with the semicircle above the x-axis. Its circle tangent at $O$ has $P=(0,1/2)$ and radius $1/2$. By reflection assume $Q=(q,0)$ with $q>0$; the second radius is $1-q$. Tangency to the first circle gives $q^2+1/4=(3/2-q)^2$, hence $q=2/3$. Write $R=(x,y)$ and its radius as $r$. The three tangencies give $x^2+y^2=(1-r)^2$, $x^2+(y-1/2)^2=(r+1/2)^2$, and $(x-2/3)^2+y^2=(r+1/3)^2$. Subtracting gives $y=1-3r$ and $x=1-2r$. Substitution yields $12r^2-8r+1=0$. The root $r=1/2$ puts $R$ below the diameter, so $r=1/6$ and $R=(2/3,1/2)$, proving the rectangle.
ratingReason: Tangency equations determine the second semicircle, then isolate the inner Soddy circle from a second algebraic root lying below the original semicircle.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the official PAMO archive; proof independently checked. Individual editorial half-step difficulty rating.

title: An altitude equal to a median
statement: In an acute triangle $ABC$, let $F$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$ and let $M$ be the midpoint of $CA$. Suppose $BM=CF$ and $\angle MBC=\angle FCA$. Prove that $ABC$ is equilateral.
solution: Put $a=BC,b=CA,c=AB$ and denote the angles by $A,B,C$. The given angle yields $\angle MBC=90^\circ-A$ and $\angle ABM=90^\circ-C$. Since triangles $ABM$ and $CBM$ have equal areas, $c\cos C=a\cos A$. The cosine rule transforms this into $(c^2-a^2)(b^2-c^2-a^2)=0$. The second factor cannot vanish because $B$ is acute. Thus $a=c$, so $BM$ is also an altitude. Computing the area with bases $AC$ and $AB$ gives $b\,BM=c\,CF$. Since $BM=CF>0$, $b=c=a$.
ratingReason: The angle condition and equal areas first force an isosceles triangle; only then does the equality of the median and altitude force all sides equal.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the official PAMO archive; proof independently checked. Individual editorial half-step difficulty rating.

title: Concurrency in a hexagon with paired equal sides
statement: A convex hexagon $ABCDEF$ satisfies $AB=BC$, $CD=DE$, $EF=FA$ and $\angle ABC=2\angle AEC$, $\angle CDE=2\angle CAE$, $\angle EFA=2\angle ACE$. Prove that $AD,CF,EB$ concur.
solution: Let $O$ be the circumcentre of triangle $ACE$. Convexity places $B$ and $E$ on opposite sides of $AC$. The isosceles condition and doubled-angle condition therefore identify $B$ as the reflection of $O$ in $AC$: on the perpendicular bisector of $AC$, that side and that subtended angle determine a unique point. Similarly $D$ and $F$ are the reflections of $O$ in $CE$ and $EA$. Use vectors with origin $O$, writing the vectors of $A,C,E$ as $a,c,e$. The reflection of the centre in a chord is twice that chord’s midpoint, so $b=a+c$, $d=c+e$, and $f=e+a$. The point with vector $(a+c+e)/2$ is simultaneously the midpoint of $AD,CF,EB$. Thus all three lines concur.
ratingReason: The doubled angles identify three reflected circumcentres; a vector identity then makes all three cevians pass through the nine-point centre.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the official PAMO archive; proof independently checked. Individual editorial half-step difficulty rating.

title: A common tangent and an angle bisector
statement: Two circles meet at $M,N$. Their common tangent touches them at $P,Q$ respectively, on the side nearer $N$. The line $PN$ meets the second circle again at $R$. Prove that $MQ$ bisects $\angle PMR$.
solution: The tangent–chord theorem in the first circle gives $\angle PMN=\angle QPN$, and in the second gives $\angle NMQ=\angle PQN$. Hence $\angle PMQ=\angle QPN+\angle PQN$. Because $P,N,R$ are collinear with $N$ between $P$ and $R$, the exterior-angle theorem makes this sum $\angle QNR$. Finally $M,N,Q,R$ are concyclic, so $\angle QMR=\angle QNR$. This proves the desired equality of the two angles. Equivalently the calculation can be performed with directed angles to cover the limiting relative positions.
ratingReason: Two tangent–chord equalities convert the desired bisection into the exterior-angle theorem in triangle PNQ.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the official PAMO archive; proof independently checked. Individual editorial half-step difficulty rating.

title: A set of people that distinguishes every club
statement: A town has 99 nonempty clubs, no two with the same membership. Find the least number $n$ such that one can always choose at most $n$ people whose membership patterns distinguish every pair of clubs.
solution: The answer is 98. Initially all clubs are in one class. If two clubs still have the same membership pattern on the chosen people, their distinct full membership lists provide a person who belongs to exactly one of them. Adding that person increases the number of pattern classes by at least one. After at most 98 additions all 99 clubs have different patterns. For sharpness, let the clubs be 99 different singleton sets. If at most 97 people are selected, two singleton clubs have no selected member and remain indistinguishable.
ratingReason: Repeatedly splitting indistinguishable clubs gives a sharp n−1 separator bound; the singleton-club example proves optimality.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

provenance.archive: University of Western Australia olympiad archive

title: Arbitrarily long progressions of perfect powers
statement: For every integer $n>1$, prove that there are $n$ positive integers in a nonconstant arithmetic progression, each a perfect power with exponent greater than 1. Also give an example with three terms.
solution: For three terms, $1,25,49$ are squares in arithmetic progression. For general $n$, choose distinct primes $q_1,\ldots,q_n$. For each prime $p\le n$, the Chinese remainder theorem supplies a nonnegative integer $e_p$ such that $e_p+v_p(i)\equiv0\pmod{q_i}$ for every $i=1,\ldots,n$. Put $M=\prod_{p\le n}p^{e_p}$. In the integer $Mi$, every prime exponent is divisible by $q_i$, so $Mi$ is a $q_i$th power. The terms $M,2M,\ldots,nM$ give the required progression.
ratingReason: A common multiplier is constructed prime by prime using simultaneous congruences on valuations, with a distinct target exponent for each term.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

provenance.archive: University of Western Australia olympiad archive

title: A sum of p squares from a square congruence
statement: Let $p$ be prime and let $n$ be an integer such that $1+np$ is a perfect square. Prove that $n+1$ is a sum of $p$ integer squares.
solution: Write $1+np=k^2$, taking $k\ge0$. Modulo $p$, $(k-1)(k+1)=0$, so $k=pt+\varepsilon$ for some integer $t$ and $\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$ (also when $p=2$). Expanding gives $n=pt^2+2\varepsilon t$. Hence $n+1=(t+\varepsilon)^2+(p-1)t^2$, an explicit sum of exactly $p$ squares.
ratingReason: A square congruent to 1 modulo a prime has a root congruent to ±1; expanding that root yields an explicit representation by p squares.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

provenance.archive: University of Western Australia olympiad archive

title: Ordered products and reciprocal sums
statement: Real numbers $x_i,y_i$ satisfy $0<x_1y_1<\cdots<x_ny_n$ and $\sum_{j=1}^i x_j\ge\sum_{j=1}^i y_j$ for every $i$. Prove $\sum 1/x_i\le\sum 1/y_i$ and determine equality.
solution: Put $A_i=\sum_{j=1}^i(x_j-y_j)\ge0$ and $w_i=1/(x_iy_i)$, so $w_1>\cdots>w_n>0$. Summation by parts gives $\sum_{i=1}^n(1/y_i-1/x_i)=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-y_i)w_i=A_nw_n+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}A_i(w_i-w_{i+1})\ge0$. Each coefficient is positive, so equality holds exactly when all $A_i=0$, equivalently $x_i=y_i$ for every $i$.
ratingReason: Summation by parts pairs nonnegative partial sums with strictly decreasing reciprocal-product weights, also identifying every equality case.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

provenance.archive: University of Western Australia olympiad archive

title: Four points on a Steiner line
statement: Points $A,B,C,A',B',C'$ lie on a circle with $AA'\perp BC$, $BB'\perp CA$, $CC'\perp AB$. For another point $D$ on the circle, let $A''=DA'\cap BC$, $B''=DB'\cap CA$, and $C''=DC'\cap AB$. Prove that these three points and the orthocentre of $ABC$ are collinear.
solution: Use complex coordinates on the unit circle, denoting vertices by lower-case letters. The orthocentre is $h=a+b+c$. Reflection in $BC$ sends a point $z$ to $b+c-bc\bar z$; thus it sends $H$ to $a'=-bc/a$, the second intersection of the altitude with the circle. Let $D_a,D_b,D_c$ be the reflections of $D$ in the three sides. Then $d_a-h=-(ad+bc)/d$, and cyclically $d_b-h=-(bd+ca)/d$, $d_c-h=-(cd+ab)/d$. Each of $ad+bc,bd+ca,cd+ab$ has conjugate equal to itself divided by $abcd$, so their ratios are real: $H,D_a,D_b,D_c$ are collinear. Reflecting the line $DA'$ in $BC$ gives $D_aH$; its intersection with the mirror line is unchanged. Hence $A''$ lies on that same line, and likewise $B'',C''$.
ratingReason: Reflecting the construction in the triangle sides reduces it to the Steiner line of a circumcircle point; the reflected orthocentre supplies the key identification.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

provenance.archive: University of Western Australia olympiad archive

title: An interior point that trisects an angle
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $\angle ACB=2\angle ABC$. A point $D$ inside the triangle satisfies $AD=AC$ and $DB=DC$. Prove $\angle BAC=3\angle BAD$.
solution: Write $\angle ABC=\beta$ and $\angle DBC=\angle BCD=t$. Then $\angle ACD=2\beta-t$, and $AD=AC$ gives $DC=2AC\cos(2\beta-t)$. Also $DB=DC$ gives $BC=2DC\cos t$. The sine rule in $ABC$ therefore yields $\sin3\beta/\sin\beta=4\cos t\cos(2\beta-t)$. Expanding both sides cancels $2\cos2\beta$ and leaves $2\cos(2\beta-2t)=1$. Because $0<\beta-t<60^\circ$, this gives $\beta-t=30^\circ$. Finally $\angle BAD=\beta-2t=60^\circ-\beta$, whereas $\angle BAC=180^\circ-3\beta$.
ratingReason: Angle variables alone leave a parameter; the sine rule plus the isosceles condition then force a 30-degree relation.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

provenance.archive: University of Western Australia olympiad archive

title: An integer-root bound for a squared polynomial
statement: Let $p(x)$ be a monic integer polynomial of degree 2003. Prove that $p(x)^2-25$ has at most 2003 distinct integer roots.
solution: If there were at least 2004, one of $p-5,p+5$ would have at least 1002 distinct integer roots $r_i$. Suppose it is $p-5$. Divide out their linear factors to get $p(x)-5=s(x)\prod_{i=1}^{1002}(x-r_i)$ with $s\in\mathbb Z[x]$. At any integer $m$ with $p(m)=-5$, the nonzero distinct integers $m-r_i$ would have product dividing $-10$. Their absolute product is at least $(501!)^2>10$, impossible. Thus every integer root belongs to $p-5$, which has degree 2003. The other sign is identical.
ratingReason: Factoring p²−25 and pigeonholing the roots forces a product of many distinct nonzero integers to divide 10.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

provenance.archive: University of Western Australia olympiad archive

title: The least value of an increasing multiplicative function
statement: A function $f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ is strictly increasing and satisfies $f(ab)=f(a)f(b)$ and $f(3)\ge7$. What is the smallest possible $f(3)$?
solution: The choice $f(n)=n^2$ attains 9. Since $f(1)=1$, we have $f(2)\ge2$. If $f(2)=2$, then $f(3)<f(4)=4$, impossible. If $f(2)=3$, monotonicity and multiplicativity give $f(27)=f(3)^3\ge343>243=f(32)$, again impossible. Thus $f(2)\ge4$, so $f(3)^2=f(9)>f(8)=f(2)^3\ge64$. As $f(3)$ is integral, it is at least 9.
ratingReason: Multiplicativity turns strategically chosen comparisons 27<32 and 8<9 into bounds ruling out f(3)=7,8.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

provenance.archive: University of Western Australia olympiad archive

title: A rotation that exchanges the two edge colours
statement: Join every pair of $n$ labelled points on a circle. Colour each segment red or blue so that rotating both endpoints one position changes its colour. (a) For which $n$ can this be done? (b) Prove any two points can be connected using at most three red segments.
solution: (a) Every edge orbit under rotation must have even length. Non-antipodal edges have orbit length $n$, and antipodal edges (when $n$ is even) have orbit length $n/2$. Hence $4\mid n$, which is also sufficient: alternate colours on each orbit. (For $n=1$ the edge-free case is vacuous.) (b) Rotation is an isomorphism between the red graph and its complement. If two vertices $x,y$ have no blue path of length at most two, then $xy$ is red and every other vertex has a red edge to at least one of $x,y$. Consequently every pair of vertices has a red path of length at most three, through $x,y$ if necessary. If no such pair $x,y$ exists, the blue graph has diameter at most two, and its isomorphic red graph does too.
ratingReason: The antipodal edge orbit determines the parity obstruction; the diameter claim then uses the relation between a graph and its complement.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

provenance.archive: University of Western Australia olympiad archive

title: Repeated inversion-count offspring
statement: For a finite sequence of nonnegative integers, replace each term by the number of smaller terms to its right. Repeat this operation. Prove that eventually the sequence stops changing.
solution: The last entry becomes 0 after one operation and stays so. Work backward by induction. Suppose all entries to the right of position $i$ have stabilised at $c_{i+1},\ldots,c_n$. Thereafter position $i$ iterates the map $h(t)=\#\{j>i:c_j<t\}$. This map is nondecreasing and takes values in $\{0,\ldots,n-i\}$. If an iterate is at least its predecessor, monotonicity makes all later iterates nondecreasing; if it is at most its predecessor, all later iterates are nonincreasing. A bounded monotone integer sequence stabilises. Thus position $i$ eventually stabilises too. Induction reaches the first entry.
ratingReason: Stabilisation propagates from the last coordinate to the first; once the tail is fixed, a coordinate iterates a bounded nondecreasing integer map.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

provenance.archive: University of Western Australia olympiad archive

title: Guessing an integer using prime sums
statement: Alice chooses an integer $a$ with $1\le a\le2006$. On each turn Bob names a positive integer $b$ and learns whether $a+b$ is prime. Prove he can always determine $a$ in fewer than 2006 turns.
solution: It suffices to separate any two remaining candidates $u<v$. Put $d=v-u$ and choose a prime $q>v$. The progression $q,q+d,q+2d,\ldots$ starts with a prime, but its term $q+qd=q(1+d)$ is composite. Let $k\ge1$ be the first index with $q+kd$ composite. Then $b=q+(k-1)d-u>0$ makes $u+b$ prime and $v+b$ composite. This query eliminates at least one of the candidates. Repeat while more than one remains. Starting from 2006 candidates requires at most 2005 queries.
ratingReason: Any two candidates can be separated by a prime/composite translate; the separating query comes from the first composite term in a finite prime-started arithmetic progression.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

provenance.archive: University of Western Australia olympiad archive

title: Parallel stages for cutting a rectangular grid
statement: An $m\times n$ grid must be cut into unit squares. In each stage, any collection of current rectangular pieces may each be cut once along a grid line. What is the minimum number of stages?
solution: The minimum is $\lceil\log_2m\rceil+\lceil\log_2n\rceil$. A cut in an $a\times b$ rectangle leaves one child whose cut dimension is at least half the previous one. Therefore the quantity $\lceil\log_2a\rceil+\lceil\log_2b\rceil$ decreases by at most 1 along a suitable chain of descendants. A unit square has value 0, proving the lower bound. For attainment, bisect the row dimension as evenly as possible in every current piece at each stage, until all heights are 1; this takes $\lceil\log_2m\rceil$ stages. Repeat in the column dimension for $\lceil\log_2n\rceil$ stages.
ratingReason: A logarithmic potential gives a lower bound by following the larger piece at each cut; parallel bisections attain it.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

provenance.archive: University of Western Australia olympiad archive

title: A multiplicative magic square
statement: A $3\times3$ array of distinct positive integers has the same product $P$ in each row, column and diagonal. Show that exactly one $P$ lies between 5000 and 6500, and construct an array attaining it.
solution: Write the entries rowwise as $a,b,c;d,e,f;g,h,i$. Multiplying the two diagonal products and the middle-row product and dividing by the first and third column products gives $e^3=P$. The only cube in the specified interval is $18^3=5832$. It is attained by the rows $(2,81,36)$, $(324,18,1)$, $(9,4,162)$. All nine numbers are distinct, and direct multiplication verifies that every row, column and diagonal has product 5832.
ratingReason: Multiplying and dividing line products forces the common product to be the central entry cubed; a nontrivial distinct-entry construction attains the sole cube in range.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

provenance.archive: University of Western Australia olympiad archive

title: When a square-free divisor sum is a multiple
statement: Let $F(n)$ be the sum of the square-free positive divisors of $n$. Determine all positive integers $n$ for which $F(n)/n$ is an integer.
solution: If the distinct prime factors of $n$ are $p_1,\ldots,p_k$, then $F(n)=\prod(p_i+1)$. Suppose the largest factor is $p>3$. Since $p\mid n\mid F(n)$, it divides $q+1$ for some prime factor $q\le p$. The only possibility is $q+1=p$, but then $q=p-1$ is even and larger than 2, a contradiction. Thus $n=2^a3^b$. If exactly one exponent is positive, $F(n)$ is respectively 3 or 4 and is not divisible by $n$. If both are positive, $F(n)=12$, so $n$ is 6 or 12. Also $n=1$ works.
ratingReason: The largest prime divisor rules out every prime above 3, after which divisibility of the square-free-divisor sum leaves only three integers.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

provenance.archive: University of Western Australia olympiad archive

title: Reducibility of a quintic with prime-power constant
statement: Find all primes $p$ and positive integers $n$ for which $x^5+x+p^n$ factors into two integer polynomials of positive degree.
solution: The sole pair is $(p,n)=(2,1)$. For a linear factor with root $t\in\mathbb Z$, $t(t^4+1)=-p^n$ and the two factors are coprime, forcing $t=-1$ and $p^n=2$. Otherwise monicity permits a quadratic factor $x^2+ax+b$. Comparing coefficients with its monic cubic quotient gives $3a^2b-a^4-b^2=1$ and $ab(2b-a^2)=p^n$. Thus $a,b$ are signed powers of $p$, but cannot both be divisible by $p$; one is $\pm1$. If $a=\pm1$, the first identity gives $b=1$ or 2, and the constant term is $\pm1$ or $\pm6$, impossible. If $b=\pm1$, the same identity forces $a=\pm1$, already excluded. Finally $x^5+x+2=(x+1)(x^4-x^3+x^2-x+2)$.
ratingReason: A complete irreducibility analysis needs both possible factor degrees; coefficient elimination in the quadratic–cubic case interacts with the prime-power constant term.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

provenance.archive: University of Western Australia olympiad archive

title: Two rows with many matching colours
statement: Every cell of a $5\times2008$ board is coloured red or blue. What is the largest integer $N$ such that two rows always agree in at least $N$ columns?
solution: The answer is 804. A column with $r$ red cells contributes $\binom r2+\binom{5-r}2\ge4$ agreements among the ten row pairs. Thus some pair has at least $\lceil4\cdot2008/10\rceil=804$ agreements. For sharpness, use 200 copies of each of the ten column patterns with exactly two red cells. Every pair agrees in exactly four of the ten patterns, so initially has 800 agreements. Append any eight different such patterns. A pair can gain at most four agreements, hence no pair exceeds 804.
ratingReason: Double-counting agreements gives the lower bound; a balanced collection of the ten two-red column patterns attains the rounded bound.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

provenance.archive: University of Western Australia olympiad archive

title: A median, bisector and two perpendiculars
statement: In triangle $ABC$ with $AB\ne AC$, points $P,Q,R,S$ lie on line $BC$: $P$ is its midpoint, $AQ$ bisects $\angle BAC$, $AR\perp BC$, and $AS\perp AQ$. Prove $PR\cdot QS=AB\cdot AC$.
solution: Take $R=(0,0),A=(0,h),B=(b,0),C=(c,0)$ with $h>0$ and $b<c$. Put $u=AB,v=AC$. If $\theta$ is the directed angle from $AR$ to $AQ$, the angle-bisector property gives $2\theta=\arctan(b/h)+\arctan(c/h)$. Thus $|\sin2\theta|=h|b+c|/(uv)$. Also $PR=|b+c|/2$. The intersections of the two perpendicular lines $AQ,AS$ with the base have coordinates $h\tan\theta$ and $-h\cot\theta$, so $QS=2h/|\sin2\theta|$. Multiplication yields $uv$. The assumption $AB\ne AC$ ensures $b+c\ne0$.
ratingReason: Resolve lengths along the base and express the two perpendicular cevians by the tangent and cotangent of one angle; a sine difference cancels the apparent complexity.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

provenance.archive: University of Western Australia olympiad archive

title: A divisor that separates four residues
statement: Let $0<a<b<c<d<2010$ be integers. Prove that some positive divisor $e<2010$ of 2010 makes their four remainders pairwise distinct.
solution: Use the four divisors $2010/p$ for $p\in\{2,3,5,67\}$. If each fails, choose a pair of the four numbers whose difference is divisible by that divisor, and label its edge by $p$. No edge can receive two labels: the least common multiple of the corresponding divisors is 2010, larger than every nonzero difference. Four distinct edges on four vertices contain a cycle. Sum the signed differences around that cycle; the sum is zero. Choose an edge labelled $p$. Every other edge difference on the cycle is divisible by $p$, whereas this edge difference is $(2010/p)t$ with $0<|t|<p$ and so is not divisible by $p$. This contradicts the zero sum.
ratingReason: Four failed maximal-divisor tests label four distinct edges of K4; a cycle gives a contradiction after reduction modulo the prime corresponding to one edge.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

title: Three vertices closer than the circumradius
statement: Three distinct points $A,B,C$ lie on a circle of radius $r$. Prove that their triangle is obtuse exactly when there is a point $X$ with $XA,XB,XC<r$.
solution: Place the centre at the origin. If such $X$ exists, then for each vertex vector $v$, $|v-X|^2<r^2=|v|^2$, so $v\cdot X>|X|^2/2>0$. All vertices therefore lie in an open semicircle. Conversely, if all lie in an open semicircle, choose a unit vector $u$ pointing into its half-plane. The three numbers $v\cdot u$ have a positive minimum; for sufficiently small $t>0$, $X=tu$ satisfies $|v-tu|^2=r^2-2t(v\cdot u)+t^2<r^2$ for all vertices. Finally, three points lie in an open semicircle exactly when the intervening opposite arc has length greater than a semicircle; the inscribed angle subtending it is then greater than $90^\circ$.
ratingReason: Translate the strict distance inequalities into a common open half-plane through the circumcentre; the semicircle criterion is then equivalent to obtuseness.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

title: A function preserving sums of two squares
statement: Determine all $f:\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ with $f(1)>0$ and $f(x)^2+f(y)^2=f(x^2+y^2)$ for nonnegative integers $x,y$.
solution: The unique answer is $f(n)=n$. Substituting $(0,0),(1,0),(1,1)$ gives $f(0)=0,f(1)=1,f(2)=2$, then $f(4)=4,f(5)=5,f(8)=8$. Whenever $t^2+u^2=v^2+w^2$ and $f$ fixes $u,v,w$, it fixes $t$, since its values are nonnegative. Use $3^2+4^2=0^2+5^2$ to get $f(3)=3$, then $f(9)=9,f(10)=10$. Next $6^2+8^2=0^2+10^2$ and $7^2+1^2=5^2+5^2$ give 6 and 7. For strong induction beyond 10, use $(2m+1)^2+(m-2)^2=(2m-1)^2+(m+2)^2$ for odd inputs, and $(2m+2)^2+(m-4)^2=(2m-2)^2+(m+4)^2$ for even inputs. All three other arguments are smaller and nonnegative. The identity function directly works.
ratingReason: Initial sum-of-two-squares identities establish a substantial base range; two further identities then support a strong induction for all inputs.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

title: Triangular numbers covering every residue
statement: Find all positive integers $n$ such that for every integer $k$ there is an integer $i$ with $i(i-1)/2\equiv k\pmod n$.
solution: The answers are the powers of 2, including 1. If an odd prime $p$ divides $n$, then modulo $p$ the indices $i$ and $1-i$ give the same triangular number, so there are at most $(p+1)/2<p$ values. Thus no such prime may divide $n$. Conversely, induct on $a$ to obtain all residues modulo $2^a$. Given an index with the desired residue modulo $2^{a-1}$, compare it with $i+2^a$: their triangular numbers differ by $2^{a-1}(2i+2^a-1)$, which is $2^{a-1}$ modulo $2^a$. These two choices give both possible lifts.
ratingReason: An odd prime factor creates a two-to-one triangular-residue obstruction, whereas shifting an index by a power of two lifts either residue class.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

title: One element as a sum of eleven selected integers
statement: Let $T\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,2211\}$ have 2011 elements. Prove that some element of $T$ is a sum of 11 elements of $T$, with repetition allowed.
solution: Let $m=\min T$. Since only 200 integers are omitted, $m\le201$. Both $T$ and its translate $T+10m$ lie in the integer interval $[m,2211+10m]$, containing $2212+9m\le4021$ integers. Their sizes add to 4022, so they intersect. Therefore $x+10m\in T$ for some $x\in T$. This is the sum of $x$ and ten copies of $m$, all selected elements.
ratingReason: The smallest selected number bounds a translate tightly enough that two sets of size 2011 must overlap; the overlap yields ten repeated summands.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

title: Points whose coordinate pairs overlap
statement: A set $S$ of points in the plane has no three collinear. For every pair $(a,b),(c,d)$ in $S$, at least two of $a,b,c,d$ are equal. What is the largest possible size of $S$?
solution: The maximum is 8. At most two points lie on $x=y$. Each remaining point gives a two-element coordinate set, and these sets intersect pairwise. Such a family either has one element common to all sets, or consists of subsets of a fixed three-element set: take two sets $\{u,v\},\{u,w\}$; a set missing $u$ must be $\{v,w\}$, which forces the claim. In the common-element case, the points lie on one horizontal and one vertical line, so there are at most four. Otherwise there are at most six ordered pairs. Add the two diagonal points to get the bound 8. For attainment, take all six ordered pairs of distinct elements of $\{0,1,3\}$; direct checking shows no three collinear. Add two points on $x=y$ avoiding the finitely many intersections with lines through existing pairs.
ratingReason: Discard at most two diagonal points, then classify pairwise-intersecting two-element coordinate sets as a star or a triangle; a generic construction attains eight.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

title: Integer zeros after composing a split polynomial
statement: A monic polynomial $p$ of degree 2012 has zero constant term and 2012 distinct integer roots. Find all integers $n$ for which $p(p(n))=0$.
solution: Every root $n$ works since $p(0)=0$. Conversely suppose $n$ is not a root and put $r=p(n)$, which must be a nonzero root. As 0 and $r$ are roots, $n\mid r$ and $n-r\mid r$. Write $r=kn$. The second divisibility gives $1-k\mid k$, hence $k=0$ or 2; only $k=2$ is possible. The two factors $n$ and $n-r=-n$ in $p(n)$ show $n^2\mid2n$, so $|n|$ is 1 or 2. But the remaining 2010 factors are nonzero distinct integers; their absolute product exceeds 2. This contradicts $|p(n)|=2|n|$. Therefore precisely the original 2012 roots work.
ratingReason: Divisibility by two root differences severely restricts any non-root preimage; the remaining many integer factors then contradict its small value.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

title: Two powers of one prime adding to a cube
statement: Find all triples $(p,a,b)$ with $p$ prime and positive integers $a\le b$ such that $p^a+p^b$ is a perfect cube.
solution: If $a=b$, the sum is $2p^a$, so $p=2$ and $a=b=3k-1$ for $k\ge1$. If $a<b$, the factors $p^a$ and $1+p^{b-a}$ are coprime. Thus $a=3k$ and $1+p^{b-a}=t^3$ for an integer $t\ge2$. Factor $p^{b-a}=(t-1)(t^2+t+1)$; their gcd divides 3. For $p\ne3$, they are coprime powers of the same prime, forcing $t-1=1$. Hence $t=2,p=7,b-a=1$. For $p=3$, we must have $t\equiv1\pmod3$; writing $t=1+3u$ shows $v_3(t^2+t+1)=1$. That factor, itself a power of 3, would then equal 3, impossible for $t\ge2$. The remaining family is $(p,a,b)=(7,3k,3k+1)$.
ratingReason: Separate equal exponents, then apply valuations to a difference of cubes; the gcd of its factors leaves only the exceptional prime 7.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

title: Three colours meeting inside a rectangle
statement: A rectangular array has at least three rows and columns. Its bottom row is red and top row green. Its left edge is blue except for the top and bottom tiles; its right edge is green except for the bottom tile. All other tiles are red, blue or green. Prove some four tiles meeting at one point contain all three colours.
solution: Form the grid whose vertices are tile centres and triangulate every elementary square with one diagonal. Along the boundary there is exactly one red-blue edge, on the left near the bottom. Count incidences between triangles and red-blue edges modulo 2. Internal edges occur twice, so the total is odd. A triangle with only red and blue vertices has either zero or two such edges; a triangle containing all three colours has exactly one. Therefore some triangle is tricoloured. Its three vertices are centres of tiles among one block of four tiles, which meet at the required point.
ratingReason: A parity count of red-blue edges in a triangulated dual grid forces a tricoloured triangle, which lies in four original tiles meeting at a point.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

title: Unit semicircle heights with zero horizontal sum
statement: Find all positive integers $n$ for which real numbers $-1<x_i<1$ can satisfy $\sum_{i=1}^n x_i=0$ and $\sum_{i=1}^n\sqrt{1-x_i^2}=1$.
solution: The answers are $n=1$ and all even $n$. For $n=1$, take $x_1=0$. For even $n$, take half the values equal to $t=\sqrt{1-1/n^2}$ and half equal to $-t$. For an odd $n>1$, consider the concave function $F=\sum\sqrt{1-x_i^2}$ on the compact polytope $-1\le x_i\le1,\sum x_i=0$. A minimum occurs at a vertex, where all but at most one coordinate are $\pm1$ (otherwise two coordinates can be moved oppositely). Since $n$ is odd, the remaining coordinate must be 0, so the minimum is 1. At a point with every coordinate strictly inside the interval and $n>1$, moving two coordinates oppositely in either direction gives strict concavity, so such a point cannot attain the minimum. Thus the required sum is strictly greater than 1.
ratingReason: Strict concavity on a fixed-sum polytope rules out odd sizes above one; symmetric pairs give every even size.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

title: Recovering the size of a triangle-free trade network
statement: A town network has between 12 and 28 vertices. Adjacent vertices have no common neighbour, while nonadjacent vertices have exactly two common neighbours. Determine the number of vertices.
solution: Fix a vertex $X$ with neighbours $T_1,\ldots,T_m$. These neighbours are independent. Every pair $T_i,T_j$ has exactly one common neighbour other than $X$; every non-neighbour of $X$ is adjacent to exactly two $T_i$. Thus these non-neighbours are in bijection with pairs $\{i,j\}$, denoted $N_{ij}$, and the order is $1+m+\binom m2$. The range gives $m=5$ or 6, hence order 16 or 22. The same argument at any vertex shows regularity. If $m=6$, the other four neighbours of $N_{12}$ must be among the six $N_{ij}$ with $i,j\in\{3,4,5,6\}$. Choose one non-neighbour, say $N_{34}$. Its only possible common neighbour with $N_{12}$ is $N_{56}$, contradicting the required two. Therefore the order is 16. Existence is verified by joining $X$ to all $T_i$, each $N_{ij}$ to $T_i,T_j$, and two $N$-vertices exactly when their index pairs are disjoint, for indices 1 through 5.
ratingReason: The common-neighbour rules impose a precise local graph structure and degree equation; ruling out degree six requires a second neighbourhood argument.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

title: A smallest flight network with two-step alternatives
statement: A finite directed graph has no pair of opposite arcs and each vertex has an outgoing arc. Every arc $A\to C$ also admits a two-step path $A\to B\to C$. Find the smallest possible number of vertices.
solution: The answer is 7. Fix a vertex $A$. For every out-neighbour $C$, the two-step condition gives another out-neighbour $B$ with $B\to C$. Hence the graph induced by the out-neighbours has positive indegree at every vertex. It contains a directed cycle, whose length is at least three because loops and opposite arcs are unavailable. Thus every vertex has outdegree at least three. If there are $n$ vertices, $3n\le n(n-1)/2$, so $n\ge7$. For attainment use vertices modulo 7, with arcs from $x$ to $x+1,x+2,x+4$. There are no opposite arcs, and each allowed difference is twice another allowed difference modulo 7: $1=4+4$, $2=1+1$, $4=2+2$. These identities supply all required two-step paths.
ratingReason: Every out-neighbourhood must contain a directed cycle, forcing outdegree at least three; a seven-vertex cyclic tournament attains the bound.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

title: Permutations with equal displacement at every position
statement: How many permutations $a_1,\ldots,a_{2004}$ of $1,\ldots,2004$ satisfy $|a_i-i|=d>0$ for every position $i$?
solution: For fixed $d$, view each residue class modulo $d$ as an increasing path of available values. The smallest vertex can only map to the next one. Conversely that next vertex must map back, since the smallest value has no other possible preimage. Removing the pair and repeating shows every path must have even length, with its adjacent vertices swapped uniquely. Writing $2004=qd+r$ with $0\le r<d$, the paths have lengths $q$ or $q+1$. Both cannot occur, so $r=0$ and $q$ is even. Thus exactly the positive divisors $d$ of 1002 work. Since $1002=2\cdot3\cdot167$, there are 8.
ratingReason: Each residue chain modulo the fixed displacement must be paired by adjacent swaps, so the displacement is a divisor of 1002 and each choice is unique.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

title: Red beads in an indivisible balanced necklace
statement: A necklace has an even number $n\ge4$ of red, blue and green beads, with equally many blue and green. It cannot be split into two strings of positive even lengths, each containing equally many blue and green beads. Determine the possible number of red beads.
solution: There must be exactly two red beads. Give blue weight 1, green weight −1 and red weight 0. Take partial sums after every two beads. No proper even-length zero-sum interval is allowed, so these partial sums are distinct except for the final return to zero. Consecutive values differ by 1 or 2 in absolute value; a zero difference would already be forbidden. For a cycle with at least three vertices, exactly two edges have odd length. To prove this, its smallest vertex has neighbours exactly one and two units larger; remove it and replace its two incident edges by the edge between these neighbours. The number of odd edges is unchanged, and induction reduces to a triangle. In the two-edge case there are either two odd edges or none; the latter would give no red beads, impossible because some adjacent blue and green pair would form a forbidden balanced string. A two-bead block has odd weight exactly when it contains one red bead; it cannot contain two reds. Hence the red count is two. This is attainable with equal positive runs of blue and green separated by the two reds: every even balanced proper interval would need both separating reds and then either no or all of each run, which is impossible.
ratingReason: Even-position partial sums form a simple cycle on the integer line with jumps at most two; such a cycle has exactly two odd jumps, accounting for the red beads.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

title: A residue avoided by all pair sums
statement: For $m\ge3$ integers $a_1,\ldots,a_m$, put $N=m(m+1)/2$. Prove that some integer $k$ is not congruent modulo $N$ to any $a_i+a_j$, allowing $i=j$.
solution: There are exactly $N$ unordered index pairs with repetition. If all residues occurred, these pair sums would be pairwise distinct. In particular the $a_i$ are distinct modulo $N$. Moreover the $m(m-1)$ ordered differences $a_i-a_j$ with $i\ne j$ would all be distinct: equality $a_i-a_j=a_k-a_l$ modulo $N$ implies equality of pair sums $a_i+a_l=a_k+a_j$, forcing the same ordered pair. None is zero. But $m(m-1)>N-1$ for $m\ge3$, so these differences cannot fit among the $N-1$ nonzero residues. This contradiction proves the claim.
ratingReason: If every pair-sum residue were present, they would all be distinct; then all ordered nonzero differences would also be distinct, exceeding the modulus.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

title: A nested recursion on positive integers
statement: Find all functions $f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ satisfying $f(n)=n-9$ for $n>2009$ and $f(n)=f(f(n+1009))$ for $n\le2009$.
solution: The unique function is $f(n)=n-9$ for $n>2009$, and $f(n)=2001+((n-10)\bmod1000)$ for $1\le n\le2009$, where the remainder is between 0 and 999. To derive it, first take $1010\le n\le2009$: both nested arguments exceed 2009, so $f(n)=n+991$. For $1001\le n\le1009$, the inner value is $n+1000$, now in the preceding interval; hence $f(n)=n+1991$. For $1\le n\le1000$, the inner argument $n+1009$ is in the first interval, so its value is $n+2000$. Applying the already determined function gives $n+2991$ when $n\le9$ and $n+1991$ otherwise. These intervals cover the domain and directly verify the formula.
ratingReason: The nested recursion must be resolved in several boundary intervals before the repeated output block and uniqueness become clear.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

title: Equal chords through the side lines and the incentre
statement: Let $I$ be the incentre of triangle $ABC$, with $AC\ne BC$. The circle through $A,I,B$ meets line $AC$ again at $X$ and line $BC$ again at $Y$. Prove $AX=BY$.
solution: Assume $AC=b>BC=a$; the other case is symmetric. Choose $X_0$ on $CA$ with $CX_0=a$. Triangle $CBX_0$ is isosceles, so $\angle AX_0B=90^\circ+\angle C/2=\angle AIB$. Hence $A,B,I,X_0$ are concyclic, and $X=X_0$. Power of $C$ with respect to this circle gives $CA\cdot CX=CB\cdot CY$, with directed lengths; therefore $CY=b$. Thus $Y$ is on ray $CB$ beyond $B$, and $AX=b-a=BY$.
ratingReason: A point on the longer side at the length of the shorter side creates an isosceles triangle whose exterior angle equals the standard incenter angle.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

title: Two external bisectors on the third side
statement: Let $I$ be the incentre of triangle $ABC$. A circle through $I$ is tangent to the circumcircle at $A$ and meets $AB,AC$ again at $P,Q$. Prove that the angle bisectors of $\angle BPQ$ and $\angle PQC$ meet on $BC$.
solution: Let $S$ be the second intersection of $AI$ with the circumcircle, let $R=AI\cap BC$, and let $E$ be the excentre opposite $A$. The tangent circles are related by the homothety centred at $A$ with ratio $AI/AS$, which carries $B,C,S$ to $P,Q,I$. Standard sine-rule formulas for the angle bisector give $AR\cdot AS=AB\cdot AC$: if $b=AC,c=AB$, then $AR=2bc\cos(A/2)/(b+c)$ and $AS=(b+c)/(2\cos(A/2))$. Also $AI\cdot AE=bc$, since $AI=r/\sin(A/2)$, $AE=r_a/\sin(A/2)$, $rr_a=\Delta^2/[s(s-a)]$ and $\sin^2(A/2)=(s-b)(s-c)/(bc)$, together with Heron’s formula. Therefore $AR/AE=AI/AS$. The same homothety sends $E$ to $R$, making $R$ the excentre of $APQ$ opposite $A$. Its two external bisectors are exactly those requested.
ratingReason: The circle tangency gives a homothety, and two non-obvious angle-bisector products show it carries an excentre precisely onto BC.
notes: Statement paraphrased from the UWA archive. Difficulty is an individual editorial assessment on the 1–10 half-step scale.

statement: How many positive integers less than $2019$ are divisible by either $18$ or $21$, but not both?
solution:
For any positive integer $n$, the number of multiples of $n$ less than or equal to $2019$ is given by
$$\left\lfloor \frac{2019}{n} \right\rfloor.$$
So there are $\left\lfloor \frac{2019}{18} \right\rfloor = 112$ multiples of $18$, and $\left\lfloor \frac{2019}{21} \right\rfloor = 96$ multiples of $21$. Moreover, since $\operatorname{lcm}(18,21) = 126$ there are $\left\lfloor \frac{2019}{126} \right\rfloor = 16$ positive integers less than $2019$ which are a multiple of both $18$ and $21$.

Therefore the final answer is
$$
\left\lfloor \frac{2019}{18} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor \frac{2019}{21} \right\rfloor - 2\left\lfloor \frac{2019}{126} \right\rfloor = 112 + 96 - 2 \times 16 = 176.
$$
ratingReason: Direct inclusion-exclusion using the lcm.
notes: MathNet transcription; original competition organiser credited in the source. Individual difficulty assessment retained unchanged; restored after removal of the 4–7 publication cutoff.

statement: Show that the number $122^{n} - 102^{n} - 21^{n}$ is always one less than a multiple of 2020, for any positive integer $n$.
solution:
Let $f(n) = 122^{n} - 102^{n} - 21^{n}$. We consider $f(n)$ in mod 101 and in mod 20 separately.

Consider $f(n)$ mod 101.

$$
\begin{align*}
f(n) &= 122^{n} - 102^{n} - 21^{n} \\
&\equiv 21^{n} - 1^{n} - 21^{n} \pmod{101} \\
&= -1
\end{align*}
$$

Consider $f(n)$ mod 20.

$$
\begin{align*}
f(n) &= 122^{n} - 102^{n} - 21^{n} \\
&\equiv 2^{n} - 2^{n} - 1^{n} \pmod{20} \\
&= -1
\end{align*}
$$

Therefore $f(n) \equiv -1$ both in mod 20 and in mod 101. Since 20 and 101 are relatively prime, this means $f(n) \equiv -1$ (mod 2020). As required. $\square$
ratingReason: Splitting the modulus as 20 times 101 makes the powers cancel in each modulus.
notes: MathNet transcription; original competition organiser credited in the source. Individual difficulty assessment retained unchanged; restored after removal of the 4–7 publication cutoff.

statement:
Find all real solutions to the equation
$$(x^{2} + 3x + 1)^{x^{2} - x - 6} = 1.$$
solution:
Let $a = x^{2} + 3x + 1$ and let $b = x^{2} - x - 6$. The only way to have $a^{b} = 1$ is if $a = \pm 1$ or $b = 0$.

- If $b = 0$, then we solve the quadratic $x^{2} - x - 6 = 0$ which has solutions $x = -2, 3$ (we would also have to check that $a \neq 0$ in this case)

- If $a = 1$, then we solve the quadratic $x^{2} + 3x + 1 = 1$ which has solutions $x = 0, -3$.

- If $a = -1$, then we solve the quadratic $x^{2} + 3x + 1 = -1$ which has solutions $x = -1, -2$ (we also have to check that $b$ is an even integer in this case)

Therefore there are a total of 5 candidate solutions: $x = -3, -2, -1, 0, 3$.
ratingReason: Only the elementary exponent-zero and base-plus-or-minus-one cases are needed, with domain checks.
notes: MathNet transcription; original competition organiser credited in the source. Individual difficulty assessment retained unchanged; restored after removal of the 4–7 publication cutoff.

statement: In triangle $ABC$, points $D$ and $E$ lie on the interior of segments $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, such that $AD = 1$, $DB = 2$, $BC = 4$, $CE = 2$ and $EA = 3$. Let $DE$ intersect $BC$ at $F$. Determine the length of $CF$.
solution:
First notice that the sidelengths of $\triangle ABC$ are $3$, $4$ and $5$. By Pythagoras this implies that triangle $ABC$ is right-angled at $B$. Now we can put the diagram on coordinate axes such that $B = (0,0)$, $A = (0,3)$ and $C = (4,0)$. Furthermore we get $D = (0,2)$ and since $E$ divides $CA$ into the ratio $2:3$ we get $E = (2.4,1.2)$, as shown in the diagram.

![A coordinate plane diagram showing triangle ABC with points D on AB, E on AC, and F on BC. The points are labeled, and lines AD, AE, DE, and BC are drawn.](https://mathnet.mit.edu/images/938072234333898a25a67f943dd7a9a6.jpeg)

Now we can calculate the slope of the line $DE$ to be $\frac{-0.8}{2.4} = -\frac{1}{3}$. This means that the equation of line $DE$ is given by $y = -\frac{x}{3} + 2$. Therefore the $x$-intercept of this line is the solution to $0 = -\frac{x}{3} + 2$. The solution is when $x = 6$, and thus $F = (6,0)$. Hence $CF = 2$.

$\square$
ratingReason: Menelaus or straightforward coordinates in the 3-4-5 triangle determine the length.
notes: MathNet transcription; original competition organiser credited in the source. Individual difficulty assessment retained unchanged; restored after removal of the 4–7 publication cutoff.

statement:
Let $a$, $b$ and $c$ be positive real numbers such that $a + b + c = 3$. Prove that
$$a^{a} + b^{b} + c^{c} \geq 3.$$
solution:
We start with a general fact about any positive real number $x$. There are two cases: either $x \geq 1$ or $x < 1$.

- If $x \geq 1$ then $x^{p} \geq x^{q}$ for any $p > q$. Substituting $p = x$ and $q = 1$ gives us $x^{x} \geq x^{1} = x$.

- If $x < 1$ then $x^{p} < x^{q}$ for any $p > q$. Substituting $p = 1$ and $q = x$ gives us $x = x^{1} < x^{x}$.

In either case we get $x^{x} \geq x$ for all positive real numbers $x$. Applying this fact for $a$, $b$ and $c$ gives us
$$a^{a} + b^{b} + c^{c} \geq a + b + c = 3$$
as required.
ratingReason: The pointwise observation x^x >= x for x>0 immediately yields the sum bound.

statement: A positive integer is called sparkly if it has exactly 9 digits, and for any $n$ between $1$ and $9$ (inclusive), the $n^{\text{th}}$ digit is a positive multiple of $n$. How many positive integers are sparkly?
solution:
For each $n = 1, 2, \ldots, 9$ there are $\lfloor 9 / n \rfloor$ different possibilities for the $n^{\mathrm{th}}$ digit. For example, there are $\lfloor 9 / 2 \rfloor = 4$ possible choices for the second digit (these being $2, 4, 6$ and $8$). Therefore the answer is
$$
\left\lfloor \frac{9}{1} \right\rfloor \times \left\lfloor \frac{9}{2} \right\rfloor \times \left\lfloor \frac{9}{3} \right\rfloor \times \left\lfloor \frac{9}{4} \right\rfloor \times \left\lfloor \frac{9}{5} \right\rfloor \times \left\lfloor \frac{9}{6} \right\rfloor \times \left\lfloor \frac{9}{7} \right\rfloor \times \left\lfloor \frac{9}{8} \right\rfloor \times \left\lfloor \frac{9}{9} \right\rfloor
$$
which equals $9 \times 4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 \times 1 \times 1 \times 1 \times 1 = 216$
ratingReason: Independent digit choices and the product rule.

statement:
Find the smallest positive integer $N$ satisfying the following three properties.  
- $N$ leaves a remainder of $5$ when divided by $7$.  
- $N$ leaves a remainder of $6$ when divided by $8$.  
- $N$ leaves a remainder of $7$ when divided by $9$.
solution:
We notice that $\{5,6,7\}$ are each $2$ less than $\{7,8,9\}$ respectively. Therefore $N + 2$ must be a multiple of $7$, $8$ and $9$. Since $7$, $8$ and $9$ are pairwise coprime, this means that
$$(N + 2) \text{ is a multiple of } 7 \times 8 \times 9 = 504.$$ 
Therefore the smallest positive possibility for $N + 2$ is $504$. Thus $N = 502$.
ratingReason: The three congruences all state that N+2 is divisible by the pairwise coprime moduli.

statement:
Let $P(x) = x^{3} - 2x + 1$ and let $Q(x) = x^{3} - 4x^{2} + 4x - 1$. Show that  
if $P(r) = 0$ then $Q(r^{2}) = 0$
solution:
Notice that $P(x) = x^{3} - 2x + 1 = (x - 1)(x^{2} + x - 1)$, and the roots of $x^{2} + x - 1$ are $\frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{5}}{2}$. Therefore the roots of $P(x)$ are  
$$1, \frac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2} \text{ and } \frac{-1 - \sqrt{5}}{2}.$$  
Notice also that $Q(x) = x^{3} - 4x^{2} + 4x - 1 = (x - 1)(x^{2} - 3x + 1)$, and the roots of $x^{2} - 3x + 1$ are $\frac{3 \pm \sqrt{5}}{2}$. Therefore the roots of $Q(x)$ are  
$$1, \frac{3 + \sqrt{5}}{2} \text{ and } \frac{3 - \sqrt{5}}{2}.$$  
So it suffices to check that $1^{2} = 1$ and that $\left(\frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{5}}{2}\right)^{2} = \frac{1 \pm 2\sqrt{5} + 5}{4} = \frac{3 \pm \sqrt{5}}{2}$.


Alternative Solution:
First notice that  
$$
(x^{3} - 2x - 1)P(x) = (x^{3} - 2x - 1)(x^{3} - 2x + 1)
$$
$$
\qquad = x^{6} - 4x^{4} + 4x^{2} - 1
$$
$$
\qquad = Q(x^{2}).
$$  
If $r$ is any root of $P(x)$ then $P(r) = 0$. This implies that  
$$Q(r^{2}) = (r^{3} - 2r + 1)P(r) = (r^{3} - 2r + 1) \times 0 = 0.$$  
Hence $r^{2}$ is a root of $Q(x)$.
ratingReason: The required composition factors immediately as a product containing P.

statement: Determine all prime numbers $p$ such that $p^{2} - 6$ and $p^{2} + 6$ are both prime numbers.
solution:
If $p > 5$ then the units digit of $p$ must be 1, 3, 7 or 9.  
- If the units digit of $p$ is 1 or 9 then the units digit of $p^{2}$ is 1. Therefore the units digit of $p^{2} - 6$ is 5. Since $p^{2} - 6 > 5$ this means that $p^{2} - 6$ is not prime.  
- If the units digit of $p$ is 3 or 7 then the units digit of $p^{2}$ is 9. Therefore the units digit of $p^{2} + 6$ is 5. Since $p^{2} + 6 > 5$ this means that $p^{2} + 6$ is not prime.  
Therefore we must have $p \leq 5$ . Hence $p$ must be 2, 3 or 5.  
- If $p = 2$ then $p^{2} + 6 = 10$ is not prime.  
- If $p = 3$ then $p^{2} + 6 = 15$ is not prime.  
- If $p = 5$ then $p^{2} \pm 6$ are 19 and 31 which are both prime.  
Therefore the only answer is $p = 5$ .

Consider the following product modulo 5.  
$$p(p^{2} - 6)(p^{2} + 6) = p^{5} - 36p \equiv p^{5} - p \pmod {5}$$  
By Fermat's Little Theorem, this product is 0 (mod 5). So if $p$ , $p^{2} - 6$ and $p^{2} + 6$ are all prime numbers then at least one of them must be equal to 5.  
- If $p = 5$ then $6p^{2} - 1 = 29$ and $6p^{2} + 1 = 31$ . This is one solution.  
- If $6p^{2} - 1 = 5$ then $p = \pm 1$ . Neither 1 nor $-1$ is prime, so this case leads to no solutions.  
- If $6p^{2} + 1 = 5$ then $p$ is not an integer. No solutions in this case.  
Therefore the only solution is $p = 5$ .
ratingReason: A single check of quadratic residues modulo 5 leaves only one prime.

statement: Let $ABCD$ be a square and let $X$ be any point on side $BC$ between $B$ and $C$. Let $Y$ be the point on line $CD$ such that $BX = YD$ and $D$ is between $C$ and $Y$. Prove that the midpoint of $XY$ lies on diagonal $BD$.
solution:
![A square ABCD with a point X on side BC, a point Y on the extension of CD beyond D, and a point E on diagonal BD such that EX is parallel to CD. The segments BX and YD are marked as equal, and EX is also marked equal to them. Lines XY and DE are drawn.](https://mathnet.mit.edu/images/e9c36b7d060c32514dda36efed47190e.jpeg)
Construct point $E$ on diagonal $BD$ so that $EX$ is parallel to $CD$. So $\angle BXE = \angle BCD = 90^\circ$. Also $\angle XBE = 45^\circ$ because $E$ is on diagonal $BD$. Therefore triangle $\triangle BEX$ is an isosceles right-angled triangle. Hence
$$EX = BX = YD.$$  
Since segments $EX$ and $YD$ are parallel and equal in length, this implies that $EXDY$ is a parallelogram. Since the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, we deduce that the intersection of $XY$ and $DE$ is the midpoint of $XY$. Therefore the midpoint of $XY$ lies on line $DE$ (which is a segment of diagonal $BD$).

Alternative Solution A:
Let $ABCD$ be the unit square, with $A = (0,1)$, $B = (1,1)$, $C = (1,0)$ and $D = (0,0)$. Now let $a = BX = DY$. This means that $X = (1,1 - a)$ and $Y = (-a,0)$. Now let $Z$ be the midpoint of $XY$. We compute the coordinates of $Z$ to be
$$Z = \left(\frac{1 + (-a)}{2}, \frac{(1 - a) + 0}{2}\right).$$
The $x$ and $y$ coordinates of $Z$ are equal, therefore $Z$ lies on diagonal $BD$.

Alternative Solution B:
Let $s$ be the side-length of the square and let $a = BX = DY$. Let $Z$ be the midpoint of $XY$. Now we apply the converse of Menelaus' Theorem to traversal $BZD$ of $\triangle XYC$.
$$\frac{XZ}{ZY} \times \frac{YD}{DC} \times \frac{CB}{BX} = 1 \times \frac{a}{s} \times \frac{s}{a} = 1.$$  
Therefore $Z$, $D$ and $B$ are colinear.
ratingReason: Midpoint coordinates in a unit square prove the assertion in one calculation.

statement: What is the maximum integer $n$ such that $\frac{50!}{2^n}$ is an integer?
solution:
$50! = 1 \times 2 \times 3 \times \dots \times 50$. Of the numbers up to $50$, we need to find how many of them are divisible by $2^k$ for each $k = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6$. There are $\left\lfloor \frac{50}{2^k} \right\rfloor$ numbers which are divisible by $2^k$ and there are $\left\lfloor \frac{50}{2^{k+1}} \right\rfloor$ which are divisible by $2^{k+1}$. Therefore there are
$$
\left\lfloor \frac{50}{2^k}\right\rfloor -\left\lfloor \frac{50}{2^{k + 1}}\right\rfloor
$$
numbers between $1$ and $50$ which are divisible by $2$ exactly $k$ times. Hence the answer we are looking for is:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left(\left\lfloor \frac{50}{2}\right\rfloor -\left\lfloor \frac{50}{4}\right\rfloor\right) + 2\left(\left\lfloor \frac{50}{4}\right\rfloor -\left\lfloor \frac{50}{8}\right\rfloor\right) + 3\left(\left\lfloor \frac{50}{8}\right\rfloor -\left\lfloor \frac{50}{16}\right\rfloor\right) + 4\left(\left\lfloor \frac{50}{16}\right\rfloor -\left\lfloor \frac{50}{32}\right\rfloor\right) + 5\left(\left\lfloor \frac{50}{32}\right\rfloor -\left\lfloor \frac{50}{64}\right\rfloor\right) \\
& = 13 + 2 \times 6 + 3 \times 3 + 4 \times 2 + 5 \times 1 \\
& = 47.
\end{aligned}
$$
ratingReason: Direct application of the exponent-of-2 formula for 50 factorial.

statement: A sequence of $A$s and $B$s is called antipalindromic if writing it backwards, then turning all the $A$s into $B$s and vice versa, produces the original sequence. For example $A B B A A B$ is antipalindromic. For any sequence of $A$s and $B$s we define the cost of the sequence to be the product of the positions of the $A$s. For example, the string $A B B A A B$ has cost $1\cdot 4\cdot 5 = 20$. Find the sum of the costs of all antipalindromic sequences of length 2020.
solution:
For each integer $0\leq k\leq 1009$ define a $k$-pal to be any sequence of 2020 $A$s and $B$s, where the first $k$ terms are $B$, the last $k$ terms are $B$, and the middle $(2020 - 2k)$ terms form an antipalindromic sequence.

Now for any $k$, define $f(k)$ to be sum of the costs of all $k$-pals. Note that any $k$-pal can be created from a $(k + 1)$-pal by either
- (A) replacing the $B$ in position $(k + 1)$ with an $A$, or
- (B) replacing the $B$ in position $(2021 - k)$ with an $A$.

Therefore the sum of the costs of all $k$-pals formed using operation (A) is $(k + 1)\times f(k + 1)$. Similarly the sum of the costs of all $k$-pals formed using operation (B) is $(2021 - k)\times f(k + 1)$. Hence
$$
f(k) = (k + 1)f(k + 1) + (2020 - k)f(k + 1) = ((k + 1) + (2020 - k))f(k + 1) = 2021f(k + 1).
$$
Now we note that there are two different 1009-pals, with costs equal to 1010 and 1011 respectively. So
$$
f(1009) = 1010 + 1011 = 2021.
$$
Now if we use the formula $f(k) = 2021f(k + 1)$ iteratively, we get $f(1010 - i) = 2021^{i}$ for each $i = 1,2,3,\ldots$. Therefore
$$
f(0) = 2021^{1010}
$$
which is our final answer.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. We will find an expression (in terms of $n$) for the sum of the costs of all antipalindromes of length $2n$. Note that a string of $A$s and $B$s of length $2n$ is an antipalindrome if and only if for each $i$, exactly one of the $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ and $(2n + 1 - i)^{\mathrm{th}}$ letters is an $A$ (and the other is a $B$).

Let $x_{1},x_{2},\ldots ,x_{2n}$ be variables. For any $1\leq a(1)< a(2)< \dots < a(k)\leq 2n$, consider the string of $A$s and $B$s of length $2n$, such that the $a(j)^{\mathrm{th}}$ letter is $A$ for all $j$ (and all the other letters are $B$). Let this string correspond to the term $t = x_{a(1)}x_{a(2)}x_{a(3)}\dots x_{a(k)}$. If $x_{i} = i$ for all $i$ then the value of $t$ is equal to the cost of its corresponding string. Now consider the expression
$$
y = (x_{1} + x_{2n})(x_{2} + x_{2n - 1})\cdot \cdot \cdot (x_{n} + x_{n + 1}) = \prod_{j = 1}^{n}(x_{j} + x_{2n + 1 - j}).
$$
If we expand the brackets then we get $2^{n}$ terms, each in the form $t = x_{a(1)}x_{a(2)}x_{a(3)}\dots x_{a(n)}$ such that for each $j = 1,2,\ldots ,n$ either $a(j) = j$ or $a(j) = 2n + 1 - j$. Therefore $y$ is the sum of all terms that correspond to antipalindromes. Hence if we substitute $x_{i} = i$ for all $i$, then the value of $y$ would be the sum of the costs of all antipalindromes. So the final answer is:
$$
\prod_{j = 1}^{n}(j + (2n + 1 - j)) = \prod_{j = 1}^{n}(2n + 1) = (2n + 1)^{n}.
$$

Let $n$ be a positive integer. We will find an expression (in terms of $n$) for the sum of the costs of all antipalindromes of length $2n$. Let $\mathcal{P}$ denote the set of all antipalindromes of length $2n$, and let $P$ be an antipalindrome chosen uniformly from $\mathcal{P}$. Note that for each $j = 1,2,\ldots ,n$ the $j^{\mathrm{th}}$ and $(2n + 1 - j)^{\mathrm{th}}$ must be an $A$ and a $B$ in some order. Let $X_{j}$ be the random variable defined by:
$\cdot\ X_{j} = j$ if the $j^{\mathrm{th}}$ letter of $P$ is an $A$ and the $(2n + 1 - j)^{\mathrm{th}}$ letter is a $B$
$\cdot\ X_{j} = 2n + 1 - j$ if the $j^{\mathrm{th}}$ letter of $P$ is a $B$ and the $(2n + 1 - j)^{\mathrm{th}}$ letter is an $A$

Notice that the cost of $P$ is given by the product $X_{1}X_{2}X_{3}\cdot \cdot \cdot X_{n}$. Now consider $f_{j}:\mathcal{P}\to \mathcal{P}$ to be the function which swaps the $j^{\mathrm{th}}$ and $(2n + 1 - j)$ letters of the string. Notice that $f_{j}$ is a bijection that toggles the value of $X_{j}$. This means that $X_{j}$ is equal to $j$ or $(2n + 1 - j)$ with equal probabilities. Therefore
$$
\mathbb{P}(X_{j} = j) = \mathbb{P}(X_{j} = 2n + 1 - j) = \frac{1}{2}.
$$
Furthermore $f_{j}$ preserves the value of $X_{i}$ for all $i\neq j$. Therefore the variables $X_{i}$ and $X_{j}$ are independent. Therefore the expected value of the cost of $P$ is given by:
$$
\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cost}(P)] = \mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{i = 1}^{n}X_{i}\right]
\qquad = \prod_{i = 1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\left[X_{i}\right]
\qquad = \prod_{i = 1}^{n}\left(\frac{1}{2} (i) + \frac{1}{2} (2n + 1 - i)\right)
\qquad = \prod_{i = 1}^{n}\frac{2n + 1}{2}
\qquad = \left(\frac{2n + 1}{2}\right)^{n}.
$$
Now the number of antipalindromes of length $2n$ is simply $2^{n}$ (one for each choice of the variables $X_{j}$). Therefore the sum of the costs of all antipalindromes of length $2n$ is simply $2^{n}$ multiplied by the expected value of the cost of $P$. This is
$$
2^{n}\times \left(\frac{2n + 1}{2}\right)^{n} = (2n + 1)^{n}.
$$

statement: Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$. Point $D$ lies on side $AC$ such that $BD$ is the angle bisector of $\angle ABC$. Point $E$ lies on side $BC$ between $B$ and $C$ such that $BE = CD$. Prove that $DE$ is parallel to $AB$.
solution:
Let $E'$ be the point on line $BC$ such that $DE'$ is parallel to $AB$. We know that $E'$ lies between $B$ and $C$ because $D$ lies between $A$ and $C$. So it suffices for us to prove that $BE' = CD$.

![A triangle ABC with AB = AC, point D on AC, and points E and E' on BC. Line DE' is drawn parallel to AB, and all relevant points are labeled.](https://mathnet.mit.edu/images/6fcf46822614183179ec509fff5df855.jpeg)

$\angle ACB = \angle CBA = \angle CE'D$.

Therefore triangle $CDE'$ is isosceles with $CD = DE'$.

$\angle E'BD = \angle DBA = \angle ADE'$.

Therefore triangle $BE'D$ is isosceles with $BE' = DE'$. Hence $CD = DE' = BE'$ as required.

statement: Let $\{x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, \ldots, x_{n}\}$ be a set of $n$ distinct positive integers, such that the sum of any 3 of them is a prime number. What is the maximum value of $n$?
solution:
First we show that $n = 4$ is possible with an example. The example $\{x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, x_{4}\} = \{1, 3, 7, 9\}$ satisfies the problem because:

$\cdot\ 1 + 3 + 7 = 11$ is prime,

$\cdot\ 1 + 3 + 9 = 13$ is prime,

$\cdot\ 1 + 7 + 9 = 17$ is prime, and

$\cdot\ 3 + 7 + 9 = 19$ is prime.

We still have to prove that $n \geq 5$ is impossible.

Consider any set $\{x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, \ldots, x_{n}\}$ such that the sum of any 3 of them is a prime number. Also consider the three "pigeonholes" modulo 3; the residue classes 0, 1 and 2. If all three pigeonholes were non-empty, then it would be possible to choose three numbers – one from each pigeonhole. This would result in a sum which is $0 + 1 + 2 \equiv 0$ (mod 3), and since the numbers are distinct positive integers, this sum would be $> 3$. Thus the sum would not be prime which is a contradiction. Hence at least one of the pigeonholes must be empty. i.e.

The numbers $\{x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\}$ are distributed amongst (at most) two different residue classes modulo 3.

Now assume for the sake of contradiction that $n \geq 5$. By the pigeonhole principle at least one residue class contains at least 3 of the numbers. The sum of any three numbers from the same residue class is always a multiple of 3 and so this is a contradiction.

Therefore $n < 5$ as required.
ratingReason: The key bound is a small residue-class pigeonhole argument modulo 3, followed by a four-element example.

statement:
Prove that
$$x^{2} + \frac{8}{x y} + y^{2} \geq 8.$$
for all positive real numbers $x$ and $y$.
solution:
Since square numbers are always non-negative we have
$$(x - y)^{2} \geq 0 \qquad \mathrm{and} \qquad (x y - 2)^{2} \geq 0.$$
Also since $x$ and $y$ are positive we have $\frac{2}{x y} > 0$. Combining this all together gives us:
$$(x - y)^{2} + \frac{2}{x y} (x y - 2)^{2} \geq 0.$$
From here we expand and simplify:
$$(x^{2} - 2x y + y^{2}) + \frac{2}{x y} (x^{2}y^{2} - 4x y + 4) \geq 0$$
$$x^{2} - 2x y + y^{2} + 2x y - 8 + \frac{8}{x y} \geq 0$$
$$x^{2} + \frac{8}{x y} + y^{2} \geq 8$$
as required.

Alternative Solution:
Consider the AM-GM inequality applied to $\left\{x^{2}, \frac{4}{x y}, \frac{4}{x y}, y^{2}\right\}$
$$\frac{x^{2} + \frac{4}{x y} + \frac{4}{x y} + y^{2}}{4} \geq \sqrt[4]{x^{2} \times \frac{4}{x y} \times \frac{4}{x y} \times y^{2}}$$
$$\frac{x^{2} + \frac{8}{x y} + y^{2}}{4} \geq 2$$
$$x^{2} + \frac{8}{x y} + y^{2} \geq 8.$$
ratingReason: A direct four-term AM–GM application gives the stated constant.

statement:
Find all triples $(x,p,n)$ of non-negative integers such that $p$ is prime and
$$2x(x + 5) = p^{n} + 3(x - 1).$$
solution:
The equation rearranges to be
$$p^{n} = 2x(x + 5) - 3(x - 1) = 2x^{2} + 7x + 3 = (2x + 1)(x + 3).$$
Since $x$ is a non-negative integer, both factors $(2x + 1)$ and $(x + 3)$ must be positive integers. Therefore both $(2x + 1)$ and $(x + 3)$ are both powers of $p$. Let
$$2x + 1 = p^{a}$$
$$x + 3 = p^{b}.$$ 
Now note that $\gcd (2x + 1, x + 3) = \gcd (x - 2, x + 3) = \gcd (5, x + 3)$ which must equal either $1$ or $5$ (because $5$ is prime). We consider each case individually:

If $\gcd (2x + 1, x + 3) = 5$ then $p = 5$ and $\min (a, b) = 1$. Thus either $2x + 1 = 5$ or $x + 3 = 5$. Either way we get $x = 2$. This leads to $p^{n} = 25$ and so $(x, p, n) = (2, 5, 2)$.

If $\gcd (2x + 1, x + 3) = 1$ then $\min (a, b) = 0$. Thus $2x + 1 = 1$ or $x + 3 = 1$. So either $x = 0$ or $x = -2$. We can't have $x < 0$ so we must have $x = 0$. This leads to $p^{n} = 3$ and so $(x, p, n) = (0, 3, 1)$.

Therefore the only solutions for $(x, p, n)$ are $(2, 5, 2)$ and $(0, 3, 1)$.

statement: A school offers three subjects: Mathematics, Art and Science. At least $80\%$ of students study both Mathematics and Art. At least $80\%$ of students study both Mathematics and Science. Prove that at least $80\%$ of students who study both Art and Science, also study Mathematics.
solution:
Let $n$ be the total number of students. Let $x$ be the number of students that study all three subjects. Let $a$ be the number of students that study Maths and Art but not Science. Let $b$ be the number of students that study Maths and Science but not Art. Let $c$ be the number of students that study Art and Science but not Maths.

So $a, b, c, x, n$ are non-negative real numbers with

$\cdot\ n \geq a + b + c + x$ (total number of students).

$\cdot\ x + a \geq 0.8 \times n$ (studying both Mathematics and Art),

$\cdot\ x + b \geq 0.8 \times n$ (studying both Mathematics and Science).

Adding all these together gives us $2x + a + b \geq 1.6 \times n$ and since $n \geq a + b + c + x$ we get:

$$2x + a + b \geq 1.6 \times (a + b + c + x).$$

Finally multiply both sides by $0.5$ and rearrange to get:

$$x \geq 0.8 \times (x + c) + 0.3 \times (a + b) \geq 0.8 \times (x + c).$$

Therefore $\frac{x}{x + c} \geq 0.8$ as required.

First note that if $x \geq 0.8n$ then $\frac{x}{x + c} \geq \frac{x}{n} \geq 0.8$.

Otherwise we have $x < 0.8n$ and so $n > \frac{5x}{4}$. Hence

$$
\frac{x}{x + c} = \frac{x}{(a + b + c + x) - (a + x) - (b + x) + 2x}
$$
$$
\geq \frac{x}{n - 0.8n - 0.8n + 2x}
$$
$$
= \frac{x}{2x - 0.6n}
$$
$$
> \frac{x}{2x - 0.6 \times \frac{5x}{4}}
$$
$$
= 0.8.
$$

statement: Let $ABCD$ be a trapezium such that $AB \parallel CD$. Let $E$ be the intersection of diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. Suppose that $AB = BE$ and $AC = DE$. Prove that the internal angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ is perpendicular to $AD$.
solution:
First note that triangle $ABE$ is isosceles because $AB = BE$.

![A trapezium ABCD with AB parallel to CD, diagonals AC and BD intersecting at E, and several angles at A, E, and C highlighted in color.](https://mathnet.mit.edu/images/935e4dd436ea123c3cec41c6e1dd10f9.jpeg)

Let $x = \angle DEC$. Angle chasing gives:
$$
x = \angle DEC = \angle BEA = \angle EAB = \angle ACD.
$$
Therefore triangle $CDE$ is isosceles. Hence $DE = DC$. Since we are also given $AC = DE$ this implies $AC = DC$. Therefore $\triangle ACD$ is isosceles. Since $x = \angle ACD$ this gives us
$$
\angle CDA = \angle DAC = 90^\circ - \frac{x}{2}
$$
Now let $\lambda$ be the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$. Since $x = \angle BAC$ we know that $\lambda$ makes an angle of $\frac{1}{2} \angle BAC = \frac{x}{2}$ with line $AC$. Therefore the angle between $\lambda$ and $AD$ is
$$
\frac{x}{2} + \angle DAC = \frac{x}{2} + \left(90^\circ - \frac{x}{2}\right) = 90^\circ
$$
as required.
